#548. Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy

Abortion laws in Poland are very restrictive. Activists there have found a new way to help women wanting to terminate a pregnancy: the "Abortomat," a locker that dispenses abortion pills. But they face fierce opposition.

Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.

Known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.

Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.

In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.

Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, showed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.

Inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.

The "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.

Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.

"When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.

Women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.

In 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.

Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.

Wydrzynska said she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.

Dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, said the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated."

She said that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.

"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she said.

The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.

"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," said Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.

Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.

At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan."

"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she said.

Earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.

Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.

"I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she said.

"I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.

Another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, said they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.

In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.

Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.

"I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she said.

After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.

Afterwards, Tusk said abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.

In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.

One reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.

The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.

Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.

According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents said they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.

Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.

#545. Teams Lock in Mission Architecture for NASA’s SR-1 Freedom

NASA completed a major review for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom and locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time.

Experts from across the agency, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), and industry met at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland for a major SR-1 mission design review in October. Several key decisions were made, propelling the mission from an early concept toward a defined spacecraft design.

“SR-1 marks a pivotal step in how we travel through the solar system,” said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director. “This mission will be the first freight run on the railroad of the solar system, and the decisions we’re making now are laying the tracks for every nuclear-powered spacecraft that follows.”

Planned for launch in late 2028, SR-1 will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall, a capsule carrying three next-generation helicopters, to Mars. Once deployed, the helicopters will study Martian geology and climate history, explore new terrain, and search for signs of subsurface ice.

As NASA prepares for more ambitious exploration missions, future spacecraft and surface operations will require significantly more power than current systems can provide, particularly in environments where sunlight is limited or unavailable. SR-1 will demonstrate how fission power can enable long-duration missions, pave the way for reliable surface power systems to support NASA’s future Moon Base, and enable exploration deeper into the solar system.

The SR-1 Freedom spacecraft design has evolved since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman first introduced the concept in March at the agency’s Ignition event, where leadership shared plans to develop a fission-powered spacecraft in time for the next Mars launch window.

One significant change is to use a shorter boom than the one shown in early illustrations. The boom separates the reactor from the spacecraft’s main body, known as the Power and Propulsion Element. The shorter boom will reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design.

NASA and DOE experts also determined that improvements in shielding and spacecraft design will allow the reactor to operate closer to the rest of the spacecraft. This will simplify integration while maintaining the radiation protection needed for spacecraft electronics and the SkyFall payload.

Teams are continuing to evaluate other key design features, including the number of radiator panels on SR-1, output power levels of its nuclear power module, and how long its reactor will operate. These decisions will help shape the final spacecraft design and ensure it meets mission objectives.

In addition, the team is modifying the spacecraft’s Power and Propulsion Element by updating its communications system for the journey to Mars. SR-1 Freedom will use larger X-band antenna dishes to send data across deep space back to Earth. Further maturation of the spacecraft plans will focus on reducing risk, simplifying the design, and staying on schedule.

NASA awarded a $39.3 million contract to Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory to develop the heat rejection system for the spacecraft’s nuclear power module. The system will remove excess heat generated by the spacecraft’s nuclear power system, allowing it to operate safely and efficiently. The lab is working with the company Advanced Cooling Technologies as a key strategic commercial partner for providing the critical heat pipe and composite radiator technologies that will enable the system to meet the demanding mission requirements.

Awarded under the Aerospace Research, Development, and Engineering Support II contract, the contract action ensures the Applied Physics Laboratory team will design, build, test, and evaluate the system, along with producing the hardware needed for flight. The heat rejection system is a key part of demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in space and will help lay the groundwork and industrial production foundation for future high-power nuclear systems used in deep space exploration.

Along with the spacecraft design, teams have defined the mission timeline and planned operations.

After launch and once the spacecraft has left Earth orbit, SR-1 Freedom will activate and gradually increase reactor power. The reactor system will operate for an initial period of time before shutting down. During this period, the spacecraft will collect and send performance data back to Earth. Solar arrays will then provide power as it cruises to Mars.

After delivering SkyFall to Martian orbit, SR-1 Freedom will restart its fission reactor, collecting additional data on the spacecraft’s performance in deep space.

“By refining the design and advancing this architecture, we’re not just building a spacecraft, we’re establishing the foundation for a new era of reliable, efficient transport beyond Earth orbit,” Sinacore said. “What we learn from SR-1 Freedom will shape the future of exploration for decades to come.”

With key design decisions advancing and teams across NASA, DOE, and industry working together, SR-1 Freedom is moving toward its 2028 launch goal. The mission will demonstrate new capabilities for nuclear-powered transportation and help establish the foundation for future exploration beyond Earth.

#544. Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret

Carbon is essential to every living thing on Earth, from microscopic organisms to humans. Yet scientists are still working to answer a fundamental question about our planet's history: Where did all this carbon originally come from?

A new study of volcanic rocks from Hawaii offers a surprising possible answer. Researchers have uncovered chemical evidence suggesting that much of Earth's carbon may have arrived aboard ancient meteorites during a particular stage of the planet's formation. Even more remarkably, the findings suggest that some of this carbon became trapped deep inside Earth's core before eventually making its way back to the surface.

The discovery centers on unusual carbon dioxide signatures preserved in volcanic rocks. Researchers believe these chemical fingerprints may reveal carbon that originated in Earth's core and traveled upward through the planet's interior.

"We think that we found evidence of carbon from Earth's core leaking into the core-mantle boundaries and traveling all the way to the surface," says lead author Yves Moussallam, an associate professor in Columbia University's Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences at Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.

The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

How Carbon Could Escape From Earth's Core

To understand how carbon might travel from Earth's deepest interior to its surface, it helps to look at the planet's internal structure.

Beneath Earth's thin outer crust lies the mantle, a vast region of mostly solid rock extending approximately 1,800 miles downward. Below that is the outer core, a roughly 1,400-mile-thick layer of molten metal surrounding the extremely hot, dense, solid metallic inner core.

Scientists believe that most of Earth's carbon is stored in its core. However, directly examining this material is far beyond the reach of current technology, and researchers may never be able to obtain samples from such extreme depths.

Fortunately, Earth's volcanic activity offers another way to investigate what lies below.

Recent studies suggest that certain elements can escape from the outer core and enter the overlying mantle. From there, they may be transported toward the surface by enormous rising columns of hot rock known as mantle plumes.

These plumes begin near the boundary between the core and mantle. As they ascend, some of the rock partially melts, producing magma that can eventually erupt through volcanoes.

When that magma cools, crystals begin to grow. Occasionally, these crystals trap tiny droplets of molten material before dissolved gases have a chance to escape. The trapped droplets, known as undegassed melt inclusions, preserve valuable chemical information about the original magma.

"These melts are fossils of the magma," Moussallam says.

Because magma contains dissolved gases, including carbon dioxide, these microscopic pockets provide scientists with a rare opportunity to study carbon that may have traveled upward from Earth's core.

Hawaiian Volcanoes Reveal an Unusual Carbon Signature

Hawaii is particularly well suited for this kind of investigation. Previous research has established that its volcanoes receive magma associated with a deep mantle plume, potentially providing access to material originating near the boundary with Earth's core.

Moussallam and his colleagues examined volcanic rocks from eruptions at Kīlauea and the Tantalus Rift. Using a recently developed analytical technique, they measured carbon isotopes preserved inside undegassed melt inclusions.

Carbon isotopes are different forms of the same element that have slightly different masses. By comparing their relative abundance, scientists can identify chemical signatures that offer clues about where carbon came from and what processes it experienced.

The Tantalus Rift samples are thought to represent magma originating near the outer margins of the mantle plume. Earlier research established that typical mantle carbon has an isotopic signature between approximately -5 and -7 per mil, a measurement expressing small differences in isotope ratios. The researchers found that the Tantalus Rift samples closely matched this expected range.

The Kīlauea samples, however, told a very different story.

Magma beneath Kīlauea is believed to originate closer to the center of the mantle plume, where material may rise from near the core-mantle boundary. In these samples, the scientists detected carbon with a much heavier isotopic signature of approximately -1 per mil.

This unusual value has rarely been observed before and differs substantially from the signature normally associated with Earth's mantle.

"This signature is very, very distinct from the normal mantle," says Moussallam. "This means it must have been contaminated by another carbon source and that source is probably carbon from the core."

Although the team considers Earth's core the most likely source, Moussallam emphasizes that the evidence is not yet definitive. Additional measurements will be necessary to establish whether the carbon truly originated there.

Ancient Meteorites May Explain Where Earth's Carbon Came From

The unusual carbon signature also provided researchers with a possible clue about events that occurred more than 4.5 billion years ago, when Earth was still forming.

According to Moussallam, the isotopic composition of carbon in Earth's core should preserve "the signature of the building blocks of Earth when it was created."

To investigate that possibility, the team compared the distinctive Kīlauea measurements with carbon signatures found in ancient meteorites. They discovered similarities to a group of meteorites called carbonaceous chondrites.

Chondrites are among the oldest known materials in our solar system, dating back more than 4.5 billion years. They preserve clues about the primitive material from which planets formed.

"All of Earth is made of chondrites," Moussallam explains. "They're the building blocks of all the terrestrial planets."

Scientists generally distinguish between two broad categories of chondrites. Noncarbonaceous chondrites formed in the inner solar system, while carbonaceous chondrites, which contain more carbon, originated in the outer regions of the solar system.

Exactly how much each type contributed to Earth's formation has remained a subject of scientific debate.

The new findings support the possibility that carbonaceous chondrites made an especially important contribution during the later stages of Earth's development.

According to the researchers' proposed explanation, these carbon-rich meteorites struck the growing planet at a time when it had become better able to retain carbon delivered by incoming material. Some of that carbon may have accumulated deep within Earth, eventually becoming part of the planet's enormous internal carbon reservoir.

Over billions of years, carbon from that reservoir could have migrated upward through mantle plumes and emerged in volcanic eruptions.

If the interpretation is correct, some of the carbon essential to life today may have arrived from the outer solar system aboard meteorites during Earth's earliest history.

A Remarkable Journey From Space to Life on Earth

Despite the intriguing evidence, important questions remain unanswered. The researchers have not conclusively demonstrated that the unusual carbon came from Earth's core or established precisely how much of the planet's carbon was delivered by carbonaceous meteorites.

"We don't really know. We need more measurements," cautions Moussallam.

Nevertheless, the findings offer a fascinating possible connection between the formation of the solar system, the inaccessible depths of our planet, and the carbon that makes life possible.

They also raise the possibility that some of the carbon found in living organisms today has followed an extraordinary path. After arriving on Earth billions of years ago, it may have become incorporated into the planet's metallic core, moved slowly upward through the mantle, and eventually returned to the surface through volcanic eruptions.

"It's fun to think about. We're made of carbon, right? To think that some of this carbon might at some point have been linked to iron in the planet's core, made it all the way to the surface from out of a volcano, and is now part of the biosphere, is very interesting."

The study was coauthored by Guillaume Georgeais, HyunJoo Lee, and Bridgett Holman of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory; Damanveer S. Grewal of Yale University; Estelle F. Rose-Koga of Institut des Sciences de la Terre d'Orléans; Allan Lerner of the US Geological Survey; Paul J. Wallace of the University of Oregon; and Natália Gauer.

“The National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 calls us to share our story of space exploration with the broadest possible audience, and our partners help us accomplish that,” said Rebecca Sirmons, general manager of NASA+ at the agency’s Headquarters in Washington. “Artemis II captured the imagination of the Artemis generation, but we are just getting started. NASA and The Greenbelt Cinema will kick off their partnership with screenings of the NASA+ original documentary “The Europa Concept,” which follows NASA’s journey to investigate the science driving future exploration of Europa, Jupiter’s icy moon. Dates for screenings will be announced soon on NASA.gov.

Future programming may include other NASA+ original content, in-person live streaming events of NASA’s Artemis missions, including the first crewed mission to the Moon under the Artemis program, additional Europa content, and more. NASA+ also will remain available for free, with no ads, through the NASA app and on the agency’s website.

Earlier this year during its Ignition event, NASA outlined a bold path forward for the agency, including increasing the cadence of Artemis missions to the lunar surface, and building the first Moon Base, among other agency priorities. #541. New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice

Researchers at the University of Sydney have created experimental nose drops that significantly improved learning and memory in older mice, bringing their performance back to levels seen in younger animals. The treatment also prevented severe memory decline in mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer's-like disease. Remarkably, the approach relies on mRNA technology similar to that used in COVID-19 vaccines.

The discovery, led by Professor Greg Neely at the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre, could open a new path toward treating conditions that affect the brain. Potential applications extend beyond Alzheimer's disease to other neurodegenerative disorders, stroke, traumatic brain injury, and rare genetic and developmental conditions.

"If we can proceed quickly to clinical trials in humans, this approach could represent a world-first non-invasive delivery system to treat Alzheimer's that bypasses the blood-brain barrier," Professor Neely said.

The idea behind the research has an unusual origin. The team drew inspiration from Daniel Keyes' science fiction story Flowers for Algernon, which explores the limits of human intelligence through experiments designed to increase intelligence in laboratory mice and people.

How mRNA Nose Drops Restore Youthful Memory

The treatment works by delivering messenger RNA (mRNA), a type of genetic instruction that tells cells how to produce specific proteins. These instructions are enclosed in tiny fat-based particles called lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which protect the mRNA and help it enter cells.

Once delivered through the nose, the mRNA instructs cells to manufacture therapeutic proteins capable of reaching the brain. In effect, the nasal tissue becomes a small drug-producing factory, creating substances that can support brain function.

"In aged mice, we saw learning and memory significantly increased, returning animal cognition to its youthful prime," Professor Neely said.

"What's exciting is that this was achieved with a simple non-invasive nasal delivery system that builds on the same underlying mRNA-LNP technology platform many people became familiar with during the COVID-19 pandemic."

The study, published in Advanced Science, used mRNA to stimulate production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). This naturally occurring protein helps neurons survive, form connections, and adapt as the brain learns and stores memories. Levels of BDNF tend to decline with aging and are also associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The results were striking. Older mice that received the nose drops performed about as well as young mice in standardized tests of working memory, spatial memory, and object recognition. These tests measure abilities such as remembering recently encountered information, navigating surroundings, and recognizing familiar objects. Untreated older animals showed the expected age-related deterioration in cognitive performance.

Nose Drops Prevent Alzheimer's-Like Memory Decline in Mice

To investigate whether the treatment might also protect against Alzheimer's disease, researchers turned to a widely used laboratory model known as 5XFAD mice. These animals carry genetic mutations that cause them to develop Alzheimer's-like brain changes and memory problems unusually early in life.

In this model, signs of Alzheimer's-related brain pathology can typically be detected by two months of age, with measurable cognitive decline appearing around four months.

The researchers began administering the BDNF-producing mRNA nose drops when the mice were two months old, around the time the disease-related changes first appeared. Treatment continued twice a week.

By four months of age, the treated mice showed no further cognitive decline, unlike the severe deterioration normally seen in this model. The findings suggest that supporting brain cells early in the disease process may help preserve cognitive abilities.

One of the most intriguing results was what the treatment did not do. Although memory and learning were protected, the researchers found no reduction in amyloid plaques, the abnormal protein deposits that accumulate in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease.

That distinction could be important because many existing Alzheimer's treatments aim to remove amyloid. The new approach instead appears to help neurons remain healthy and functional despite the presence of these deposits. If the same effect can eventually be demonstrated in people, the two treatment strategies might be used together.

"Current Alzheimer's treatments largely focus on clearing these amyloid plaques," Professor Neely said. "However, just under a third of Alzheimer's patients have serious plaques but do not suffer from dementia, and these patients show naturally higher BDNF levels, suggesting if we raise BDNF, it's possible to live with Alzheimer's disease pathology."

"Our approach seems to work not by clearing plaques but by supporting the health, survival and connectivity of neurons themselves. It raises the possibility these therapies could eventually work alongside each other."

Bypassing the Blood-Brain Barrier Through the Nose

Getting medicines into the brain is one of the biggest obstacles in developing treatments for neurological diseases. The blood-brain barrier acts as a protective filter, preventing many potentially harmful substances in the bloodstream from entering delicate brain tissue. Unfortunately, it also blocks numerous drugs that scientists would like to use to treat brain disorders.

The nose offers a possible alternative route. Connections between the nasal cavity and the central nervous system may allow certain therapeutic substances to reach the brain without requiring surgery or injections directly into the brain or spinal cord.

"This is a very exciting proof of concept for a method to deliver mRNA-encoded cargo to the nervous system directly through the nose," Professor Neely said.

The team adapted mRNA technology built on the same clinically validated BioNTech platform used for COVID-19 vaccination. Instead of delivering instructions that prompt an immune response, the modified system provides instructions for producing proteins intended to benefit the brain.

First author Dr. Maria Bergamasco, from the University of Sydney's School of Life and Environmental Sciences, explained that the findings illustrate how mRNA technology could be used for purposes far beyond preventing infectious diseases.

"The success of mRNA vaccines showed these systems can safely deliver genetic instructions to cells," Dr. Bergamasco said.

"We wanted to see whether we could adapt that technology to deliver beneficial proteins to the brain in a completely non-invasive way."

Treatment Stimulates New Brain Cell Growth

The researchers also detected increased neurogenesis, the process through which new neurons are formed, in the hippocampus. This part of the brain plays an essential role in learning and memory and is particularly vulnerable to damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The increase in new neurons provides another possible explanation for the improvements in cognitive performance. By promoting the health and adaptability of brain cells, BDNF may help maintain the neural networks needed for learning and remembering information.

The nose drops also appeared to be well tolerated. Researchers reported no major side effects in the mice during the study, although further testing will be needed to establish long-term safety.

Despite the encouraging results, Professor Neely emphasized that the treatment remains experimental. So far, its effectiveness has been demonstrated only in mice, and additional animal safety studies are required before clinical testing can begin.

"Before we can trial this therapy in patients, we need to perform a series of safety studies in animals," he said. "It is a very promising pathway, but human noses are different from mouse noses, so we will need to test our drugs in humans before we know whether it will work."

That anatomical difference is a significant consideration. A delivery method that successfully transports therapeutic substances from the nasal cavity to the brain in mice may not work in exactly the same way in humans.

Nevertheless, the researchers believe the potential applications could be substantial. Beyond protecting against Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline, the technology might eventually help support memory and other mental abilities during normal aging.

"We believe our new drug, if it works in humans, can promote general cognitive health as people age, should help treat a variety of neurodegenerative diseases, and may even increase cognitive abilities in healthy young people," Professor Neely said.

The next steps involve refining the nasal delivery technology and conducting further studies to determine its safety and effectiveness over longer periods. The team hopes to advance toward human clinical trials as quickly as the required testing allows.

"Based on previous clinical trials, we know the components used in this study to be safe in humans," Professor Neely said. "We hope we can move quickly through the requisite safety studies and trial this treatment in humans in the next two years."

Although the individual components have previously been used in humans, the complete nasal treatment still requires its own safety evaluation. Whether it can deliver similar memory benefits in people remains an open question.

The project brought together researchers from the Dr. John and Anne Chong Lab for Functional Genomics in the School of Life and Environmental Sciences, the Charles Perkins Centre, and the University of Sydney's Faculty of Medicine and Health.

Greg Neely and Maria Bergamasco are listed as inventors on a provisional patent application associated with the research. The other authors reported no competing interests.

Financial support came from the National Health and Medical Research Council, the NSW Ministry of Health, and an ongoing philanthropic contribution from Dr. John and Anne Chong supporting the Neely Lab's research. The authors also acknowledged the Sydney Imaging Facility for its assistance.

All animal experiments were approved by the University of Sydney Animal Ethics Committee and conducted in accordance with the Australian Code of Practise for the Care and Use of Animals for Scientific Purposes.

#540. German economy returns to growth, so why is the country still worried?

The German economy is growing again, albeit slightly. However, economists warn that without reforms, higher productivity and solid public finances, a loss of prosperity and growing debt threaten future generations.

Is Germany's economy back on the up? The answer to that question depends on your perspective.

At the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen. "A year ago, I said here: We are angry. Today I must say: We are stunned," Bertram Kawlath, president of the Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA), said in his opening remarks on Tuesday.

The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades. It once employed more than a million people; now 15,000 positions are being cut every month. Production has shrunk about 20% since 2018.

Kawlath criticized the federal government's infighting and lack of reform, as well as what the companies consider a continued high bureaucracy and tax burden.

"[We are] stunned by the whitewashing in so many government statements. Stunned by the increasingly visible decline of our country as a business location."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised quick reforms and a rapidly noticeable economic upswing when he took office in May 2025. A year and a half later, reality has caught up with him.

Merz's coalition of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union, (CSU), along with the center-left Social Democrats(SPD), keeps running into trouble. In addition, there are crises and wars. The German economy is facing more headwinds than seldom before, Merz said in October at the German Employers' Day conference in Berlin.

Given the circumstances, small successes are even more meaningful. "A heartfelt thanks for the good news you bring," Merz said when he received the autumn report of the Council of Economic Experts in Berlin, which predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027.

The economic experts have a German government mandate to independently analyze business activity and make recommendations for economic policy. Earlier this year, they were much more pessimistic.

"The German economy has recovered quicker than expected from the energy price shock sparked by the war in Iran," said Monika Schnitzer, chair of the expert advisory board, explaining the prognosis. "We see a significant economic recovery, driven by surprisingly strong exports and high government spending."

The chancellor, who celebrated his 71st birthday on November 11, spoke of "encouraging signals" in his address. "The economy in Germany is slowly on the rise again. Considering the many crises in Germany, it was not totally expected that we would manage that."

But these improved prospects do not change the long-term problems. An ageing society means the bills for pensions, health and caregiving are constantly rising.

At the same time, the number of working-age people who finance these services is sinking. That puts increasing pressure on the public purse. According to Berlin's financial planning, social welfare costs, defense and interest on debt will account for 80% of the spending in the federal government's budget.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"We must realize that in the long term the expected revenues in the federal budget will not be enough to cover the planned expenses," Schnitzer warned. The growth rates are far below what is needed to secure the same level of prosperity as previous decades in the long term.

"To grow out of this budgetary predicament, we would need levels of economic growth which we haven't experienced in Germany for the past 50 years," she said.

The government is currently in final deliberations over its 2027 budget; spending upwards of €555 billion ($615 billion) is planned. Because revenue won't be enough to cover it, the government is planning to take on more than €118 billion in new debt. Adding the debt-financed special funds for infrastructure and the military, the new borrowing adds up to almost €204 billion.

The economic experts have warned that if Germany continues with this path, the debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 100% by 2040. This ratio indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output. At the end of 2025, it was 63.5%.

Germany is the only country of the world's leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) to still hold a AAA rating, the best possible credit rating in finance markets. It signals to investors the smallest possible default risk for German government bonds. "I want it to stay that way," Merz emphasized.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, taking on less debt will not be simple. "A reduction in debt-based financing presents policymakers with a consolidation task of historic proportions and will require tough decisions," said Schnitzer. The belt-tightening must, however, be designed to enable growth. Some recommendations include reducing environmentally harmful tax benefits — like the energy tax breaks for diesel fuel.

The so-called "mothers' pension", a pension subsidy for older parents, should be revoked, said the experts. Tax increases could become necessary in the medium term, for example with value-added tax.

"The burden should be shared fairly between generations and societal groups," Schnitzer said.

According to the chancellor, the experts' message has been received. Solid state finances are an issue in Germany but also throughout the European Union. Merz said there needs to be a consolidation course, adding that politicians have a duty to the younger generation. Reforms are needed, especially when it comes to social security systems.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Economic researchers are setting their hopes on increasing companies' productivity. Put simply, productivity describes how much a company can generate with its employees, machinery and resources in a set time.

According to the Council of Economic Experts, there is enormous variation even within the same industries. In Germany, the top companies are up to five times as productive as the weakest enterprises.

If the less productive companies caught up, economic growth could increase significantly, it said in the report. "New technologies and business models could drive peak productivity and allow new highly productive companies to develop."

But innovations need capital. It's here that the Ifo Economic Research Institute sees considerable deficiencies.

New evaluations show that German universities produce significantly fewer successful business startups than their counterparts in the United Kingdom or United States. For example, for every 1,000 students, about 14 venture capital-backed founders emerge from the vicinity of Stanford University each year. In Cambridge, the European leader, it's 3.5. In Munich, by contrast, it's only 0.5.

There continues to be an abundance of inventors and tinkerers in Germany, especially in mechanical engineering. However, the message from the industry summit in Berlin was that for renewed success, labor costs must come down. Suggestions included longer working hours and more flexibility for employers around job protection.

The intention was not to cut employees' wages and salaries. However, a new study by the German Economic Institute commissioned for the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association showed that extending the working week by an hour alone would increase real gross domestic product by 1.5% in the coming five years.

This article was originally written in German.

#539. Georgia’s Pecan Belt

Since an early-1900s planting boom, orchards along the Flint River in southwest Georgia have become a center of U.S. pecan production.

From the star of its namesake pie to a supporting player in countless side dishes, the pecan has earned a place on Thanksgiving tables across the United States. But before it becomes candied, chopped, or baked, it hangs from the branches of Carya illinoinensis—a species of hickory in the walnut family native to North America. Many U.S.-grown pecans come from orchards in Georgia, the state that has historically led the nation in production.

One hotspot of pecan cultivation is in the southwest part of the state, around Albany, in Dougherty County. The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 captured this image of the area and neighboring counties on October 23, 2026. That date falls within the pecan harvest season, which typically runs from October into December. In addition to pecans, other crops such as peanuts, cotton, and corn are also grown in the area.

Landsat observations like these contribute to the Cropland Data Layer, an annual map of crop types across the contiguous United States produced by the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Agricultural Statistics Service. The 2025 map shows pecan groves clustered along the Flint River within the Coastal Plain. Pecan trees need abundant water, and they generally do well in the area’s well-drained sandy soils that sit above the Floridan aquifer system that growers can tap for irrigation.

In the late 1800s, Georgia had less than 100 acres (40 hectares) of pecan orchards. Then, in the early 1900s, southwest Georgia’s Dougherty and Mitchell counties underwent a pecan boom when thousands of acres were planted and sold to investors. By the end of the 1950s, Georgia led the nation in pecan production, producing over 17 million pounds, according to 1959 agricultural census numbers.

In recent decades, pecan production has grown in other states, such as New Mexico and Texas. Georgia faced challenges after Hurricane Michael damaged orchards in October 2018, and Hurricane Helene dealt another blow when it swept inland in September 2024. Even so, USDA numbers show that the state’s production has topped 100 million pounds in each of the past three years (2023-2025).

In 2026, a wet summer in parts of the state helped scab take hold. The fungal disease causes brown spots on pecan twigs, leaves, and nut shucks. Meanwhile, some growers still recovering from Hurricane Helene reported the return of a solid crop.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Kathryn Hansen.

#538. Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

About 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again. According to new research, this slow buildup of ice may have marked the beginning of Earth's next glacial period, commonly called an ice age. But something unexpected happened. By the 1960s, rising summer temperatures had reversed the trend, causing the ice to retreat instead of grow.

The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a new ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years.

"It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," says Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "It's a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system."

Ancient Arctic Ice Reveals a Surprising Climate History

In a study published in Science, Young and fellow Lamont geochemist Joerg Schaefer, along with their colleagues, investigated the history of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. This enormous mass of ice covered much of Canada and the northern United States between approximately 95,000 and 20,000 years ago.

At its greatest extent, the Laurentide stretched from north of the Arctic Circle all the way south to Illinois. In some locations, its ice was more than two miles thick. Although most of this enormous ice sheet disappeared as the climate warmed, one surviving piece remains.

Known as the Barnes Ice Cap, this ancient remnant sits on central Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada, and covers an area roughly the size of Delaware.

"People always say that it disappeared, but that's not true," says Young.

Scientists already knew that the Laurentide Ice Sheet had repeatedly grown and retreated during the roughly 2.6 million years since extensive continental glaciation began in North America. What remained uncertain was whether the ice sheet had ever become smaller than it is today before expanding again.

Answering that question could reveal whether a new cycle of glaciation had begun much more recently than scientists previously believed.

(A note on terminology: Technically, we are still living in an ice age-the Late Cenozoic Ice Age-which started about 34 million years ago. Within it, colder glacial periods alternate with warmer interglacial ones, including the one we live in now. What people casually call an "ice age" is usually a glacial period. The last glacial period ended about 11,700 years ago.)

Ancient Plants Preserved Beneath Ice Hold the Clues

Piecing together the history of an ice sheet is particularly challenging when researchers are looking for evidence of its smallest extent and earliest stages of regrowth. As glaciers advance, they frequently scrape across the land, destroying the geological traces that could reveal where and when the ice first began spreading.

The Barnes Ice Cap, however, offers an unusual opportunity to investigate this history.

Unlike most glaciers, it is frozen directly to the bedrock beneath it and does not slide across the landscape. As a result, plants that once grew in areas later covered by expanding ice can remain preserved in place for thousands of years.

Since the Barnes Ice Cap began retreating in 1960, previously buried vegetation has gradually emerged from beneath the melting ice. Researchers can collect these ancient plant remains and determine when they were alive using radiocarbon dating.

This technique measures carbon-14, a harmlessly radioactive form of carbon that living organisms absorb from the atmosphere. Once an organism dies, its carbon-14 begins breaking down at a predictable rate. By measuring how much remains, scientists can estimate when the plant stopped growing and became buried beneath the ice.

These dates provide a record of when the advancing glacier covered different parts of the landscape.

"If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants. You're actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin," says Young.

Earth's Next Ice Age May Have Begun 2,000 Years Ago

The research team examined ancient vegetation uncovered by the retreating Barnes Ice Cap, along with plant remains exposed beneath smaller ice caps that have recently melted in the surrounding region.

Together, these samples allowed the scientists to reconstruct thousands of years of glacial change.

Their results indicate that the Laurentide Ice Sheet reached its smallest extent approximately 3,000 years ago. Then, around 2,000 years ago, temperatures became cold enough for the remaining ice to begin expanding again.

Young and his colleagues argue that this renewed growth should be recognized as the start of Earth's next glacial period.

That interpretation differs from previous research based on climate models, which has generally suggested that the next glaciation would not begin for thousands or even tens of thousands of years.

The disagreement partly comes down to how scientists define the beginning of a glacial period. Rather than waiting until enormous ice sheets have spread across continents, Young's team proposes that the first sustained expansion of an existing ice sheet should mark the starting point.

Under that definition, the next glaciation had already begun long before modern scientists recognized it.

The discovery also casts new light on a controversial scientific debate from the 1970s, when some climate researchers suggested that another ice age might be approaching.

"It actually was happening," Young says. "They couldn't quite prove it, but now we sort of have the evidence."

However, this early expansion would not have produced an immediate or dramatic transformation of the planet. According to Young, it would have taken thousands of years for the cooling to become noticeable and roughly 30,000 years for the Laurentide Ice Sheet to regain its enormous continental dimensions.

The process was only in its earliest stages when the warming climate brought it to a halt.

Global Warming Reversed the Growth of the Ice Sheet

By the 1960s, conditions had changed enough that the Barnes Ice Cap was losing more ice during the summer than it could replace through winter snowfall.

Instead of continuing to expand, the ancient ice began shrinking.

According to the researchers' interpretation, this reversal effectively ended the developing glacial period before it could progress into a full-scale ice age.

The consequences may extend far beyond the present day. Models projecting the future of the Barnes Ice Cap indicate that it could disappear entirely within the next few centuries.

"That will be the true very last remains of the Laurentide, disappearing for good," Young says.

The Loss of an Ancient Ice Cap Could Change Future Ice Ages

The disappearance of the Barnes Ice Cap could also have implications for how future glacial periods develop.

In the past, the Laurentide Ice Sheet provided a starting point for renewed glaciation whenever Earth's climate cooled sufficiently. Because a large existing mass of ice helps create conditions favorable for further ice accumulation, it can trigger reinforcing processes that allow glaciers to expand.

Scientists describe this kind of process as a positive feedback. In this case, existing ice helps promote the growth of additional ice, allowing an ice sheet to become increasingly extensive as temperatures remain cold.

Without the Laurentide's last surviving remnant, a future glacial period might unfold differently.

Researchers cannot yet determine when another glaciation could begin under atmospheric conditions influenced by elevated greenhouse gas concentrations. If enormous continental ice sheets eventually start forming again, they may have to develop without the ancient ice that previously helped initiate their growth.

The findings suggest that global warming has done more than melt glaciers and shrink existing ice sheets. It may have interrupted a glacial cycle that was already beginning, while also removing a feature that helped sustain ice age cycles across North America for millions of years.

"What has been an extremely natural and predictable phenomenon is now gone," says Young.

#534. AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

Research suggests that students who aren't careful about how they use ChatGPT and other AI tools risk poorer academic outcomes. It's a huge challenge for teachers.

Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.

Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.

In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

Even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.

Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she said.

Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

"Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments."

With participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with new material," Schleicher explained.

Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.

US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.

But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

91% of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.

The last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.

The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.

Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.

"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," said Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.

Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students."

That's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.

In more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

German teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.

"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she said.

There are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.

But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.

The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.

In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, said: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular."

Both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.

It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.

Müller said one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

#532. 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick

A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea. Researchers have discovered two distinct waterproofing recipes, including one that combined pine tar with beeswax. Even more remarkably, microscopic pollen grains preserved in the sticky coatings offer clues to where the ship was built and repaired during its lifetime.

For as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms. Despite their name, shipworms are actually marine mollusks that burrow into wood and can cause extensive structural damage.

Yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components. The protective materials that made these ships seaworthy received comparatively little attention, and waterproofing substances remain an understudied aspect of ancient maritime technology.

In a new study published in Frontiers in Materials, researchers from France and Croatia investigated the protective coatings of Ilovik-Paržine 1, a ship dating to the Roman Republic that sank approximately 2,200 years ago off the coast of modern Croatia.

"In archaeology little attention is paid to organic waterproofing materials. Yet they are essential for navigation at sea or on rivers and are true witnesses of past naval technologies," said first author Dr. Armelle Charrié, an archaeometrist at the Laboratory of Mass Spectrometry of Interactions and Systems in Strasbourg. "Studying the coatings, we found two different kinds on this vessel: one made of pine tar, also called pitch, and the other of a mixture of pine tar and beeswax. Analysis of pollen in the coating made it possible to identify the plant taxa present in the immediate environment during the construction or repairs of the ship."

Since its discovery in 2016, the shipwreck and its cargo have been the subject of several scientific investigations. However, this is the first study to combine molecular analysis with the examination of ancient pollen to determine both the composition of the ship's waterproofing materials and the types of vegetation growing nearby when those coatings were produced or applied.

The research brought together specialists from the Department for Underwater Archaeology of the Croatian Conservation Institute and the 'ADRIBOATS' program of the Centre Camille Jullian at Aix-Marseille University in France.

"Some regions throughout the Adriatic have particular characteristics that led local populations to develop a specific shipbuilding style," said Charrié. "Only studies like ours offer an overview into these traditions which bear witness to genuine know-how and diverse traditions."

To uncover the ancient waterproofing recipes, the researchers examined the physical structure, molecular composition, and pollen content of the coatings. Among the techniques they employed was mass spectrometry, a powerful analytical method that allows scientists to identify substances and measure their abundance based on the masses of their molecular or atomic components.

An Ingenious Combination of Pine Tar and Beeswax

The team analyzed 10 samples of the ship's protective coating to determine the biological origins of the ingredients. Distinctive chemical signatures characteristic of pine trees appeared throughout the samples, revealing that the primary waterproofing material was pitch derived from heated conifer resin or tar.

Pitch is a thick, sticky substance that has been used for centuries to seal wooden vessels and protect them from water. When heated, it becomes easier to spread over surfaces and into gaps between wooden components.

One sample, however, contained evidence of a different recipe. Ancient shipbuilders had combined the pine tar with beeswax, creating a protective substance known to Greek shipbuilders as zopissa.

The addition of beeswax made the coating more flexible and easier to apply while hot. Flexibility would have been a valuable property aboard wooden ships, whose timbers could shift and flex as they encountered waves and changing environmental conditions.

Ancient Pollen Preserves a Record of the Ship's Past

The sticky nature of pitch gave it another remarkable property that ancient shipbuilders probably never considered. It could capture tiny airborne pollen grains from surrounding vegetation and preserve them for thousands of years.

Different plants produce pollen with distinctive shapes and structures, allowing scientists to identify the types of vegetation present in an area long after the plants themselves have disappeared. By examining both the variety and relative abundance of pollen grains embedded in the ship's coatings, the researchers narrowed down the possible locations where the pitch was manufactured or applied during repairs.

The pollen preserved aboard Ilovik-Paržine 1 pointed to a surprisingly diverse range of landscapes. Some of the plant species were characteristic of Mediterranean and Adriatic coastal areas and valleys, including forests dominated by holly oak and pine. Others were associated with matorral, a type of Mediterranean shrubland that can contain olive and hazel trees.

The discovery of alder and ash pollen suggested the presence of vegetation growing near rivers or coastlines, either close to the sea or farther inland. Smaller quantities of fir and beech pollen pointed to mountainous environments. Such vegetation is characteristic of the northeastern Adriatic coast, where the mountains of Istria and Dalmatia rise not far from the shoreline.

Evidence of Multiple Repairs Across the Mediterranean

The distribution and composition of the protective materials also revealed that the vessel likely received four or five distinct batches of waterproofing coatings.

The stern, or rear of the ship, and its central section shared the same coating. At the bow, or front of the vessel, researchers identified three batches that differed from one another. These variations suggest that the ship may have undergone a series of repairs using materials obtained from different locations around the Mediterranean.

Earlier investigations of the ship's ballast, the heavy material carried aboard a vessel to improve its stability, identified the ancient city of Brundisium as its likely place of construction. Known today as Brindisi, the port city lies on the southeastern coast of Italy and was an important maritime center in the ancient Roman world.

The new pollen evidence suggests that some of the waterproofing coatings were applied in the vicinity of Brundisium. Other layers may have been added along the northeastern Adriatic coast, near the region where the vessel ultimately sank.

The findings demonstrate how microscopic biological traces can reveal aspects of ancient maritime history that might otherwise remain hidden. Even when waterproofing materials appear chemically identical, the pollen trapped within them can preserve evidence of separate repair events and the environments in which they occurred.

"While it seems obvious that ships sailing long distances need repairs, it's simply not easy to demonstrate this," concluded Charrié. "Pollen has been very useful in identifying different coatings where the molecular profiles were identical."

Materials provided by Frontiers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#530. Mike Schur reveals how Digs best life advice doubles as great writing advice

In the last moments of Dig's premiere, archaeologists Elise (Amy Poehler) and Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan) stumble upon an astounding discovery. At the bottom of a trench that no archaeologist has touched in a decade, under a thin layer of dirt, there lie the remains of a perfectly preserved statue.

"We dug in this trench for two years," Elise marvels. "And if we had only gone an inch deeper..."

She trails off, but the sentiment is clear: If the dig team had kept chipping away at the trench, they would have found the artifact of a lifetime. This scene is Dig's core thesis in a nutshell: You can always dig deeper and find greater rewards, whether it's in your relationships, your career, or yes, the giant trenches peppering an archaeological dig.

"Digging a little deeper is just good life advice in general, but it's also a really good lesson in writing," Dig co-creator Mike Schur told Mashable over a Zoom interview.

Writing, as Schur can attest, is "exhausting" work. "By creative standards, not digging a ditch standards," he noted. That means that it can sometimes be tempting to take the easy way out. To leave the trench after two years of digging, as it were.

"When you hit on something like a joke or a scene or a character that's pretty good, every ounce of your being is like, 'It's good. Just move on,'" Schur said.

However, Schur learned to curb that impulse while writing on the American version of The Office, which was developed by his mentor, Greg Daniels.

During script revisions, Schur recalled the writers' room going over scenes time and again with a fine-toothed comb, punching up jokes, pitching new ideas, and just generally refining what was on the page.

After revisions, Schur said, "I remember [Daniels] would say, 'Okay, I think that's two percent better."

Schur continued: "He used to say that if you make every joke in the episode two percent better, then the whole episode is going to be seven and a half percent better, and that's amazing. You just made something a little better and a little more memorable."

Think of that two percent as being the last little inch of dirt separating Elise from the miraculously intact Greek statue. It might be tough to excavate any further, especially if you've already been digging fruitlessly for years. But for writers, established and aspiring alike, couldn't that extra little bit of effort be worth it if you eventually strike gold?

As Schur put it, "Digging a little, doing a little extra work, revisiting a scene one more time to make it a little better is the essence of what I think differentiates memorable writing from very good writing."

#527. Cant wait for Spotify Wrapped 2026? Heres how to check your listening stats now

We're officially in the final stretch before Spotify Wrapped 2026, which means it's almost time to find out which artists, songs, and albums have been soundtracking our lives for the past year.

Maybe you're curious whether your favorite artist has held onto the top spot. Maybe you've spent the year branching out into new genres and genuinely have no idea what your listening habits look like anymore. Or maybe you're just impatient. (Understandable.)

While Spotify Wrapped 2026 isn't here just yet, you don't have to wait until December to get a glimpse of your listening habits. Spotify has its own built-in listening statistics, and several third-party services offer even more detailed insights into your musical obsessions.

Here's how to check your Spotify stats before Wrapped arrives.

You might not realize it, but Spotify already has a feature that lets you check which artists and songs you've been listening to the most.

Introduced in November 2025, Spotify's Listening Stats feature gives Free and Premium users a personalized snapshot of their recent listening habits, including their top artists and songs from the past four weeks. The feature also offers weekly highlights, which might celebrate a listening milestone, a new musical discovery, or a particularly devoted fan moment.

Open Spotify on your iPhone or Android device.

Tap your profile picture in the top corner of the screen, or swipe left to open the menu.

Explore your top artists, songs, and personalized listening insights.

Tap "Share" to post your results on social media or send them to friends.

The feature is available in more than 60 markets, although availability and the insights shown may vary.

The catch? Listening Stats focuses on your recent activity, not your entire year. So while it can tell you which artists you've listened to most lately, it won't necessarily predict your official Wrapped rankings.

If you're looking for something a little more comprehensive, stats.fm is one of the better-known third-party tools for analyzing your Spotify listening habits.

After connecting your Spotify account, you can explore your most-played artists, tracks, and genres across different time periods.

For more detailed statistics, such as actual play counts and minutes listened, stats.fm also supports importing your extended Spotify streaming history.

Connect your Spotify account and authorize the requested permissions.

Select a time range to explore your listening habits.

If you've been wondering whether your favorite artist is still your most-played act of the year, this might help you make an educated guess.

Just remember that stats.fm isn't Spotify Wrapped. Its rankings and tracking periods may differ from Spotify's official year-end calculations.

Want something a little more fun? Try Receiptify, a web app that transforms your top songs into a receipt-style graphic.

Instead of a colorful Wrapped slideshow, you'll get something resembling a shopping receipt, complete with your most-listened-to tracks.

Sign in and authorize access to your listening data.

Generate your receipt and save the image to share.

It's a particularly fun option if you're looking for something to post to your Instagram Story while everyone waits for the official Wrapped graphics to arrive.

Receiptify isn't designed to replicate Spotify's complete Wrapped experience, but it does offer a quick, shareable look at the songs you've had on repeat.

Unfortunately, no. While Spotify and third-party services can show you various listening statistics, there's no official way to access your complete Spotify Wrapped 2026 before Spotify releases it.

And even if your top artists on stats.fm look convincing, don't be surprised if your Wrapped rankings turn out differently.

Spotify uses its own methodology to calculate Wrapped results. For example, the company explained in 2025 that top songs are ranked by eligible plays, while top artists are determined using a weighted stream count that gives primary artists more credit than featured performers. Wrapped also uses a specific listening window. In 2025, Spotify counted listening activity from January through mid-November, rather than the full calendar year.

Third-party tools may use different date ranges or ranking methods, meaning their results won't always match.

Still, checking your stats ahead of time can be a fun way to see how your musical tastes have evolved over the year. Think of it as a sneak peek before Spotify delivers its annual judgment on your listening habits.

And if the results surprise you? Well, at least you'll have a little time to emotionally prepare yourself before sharing them with everyone you know.

#523. Jensen Huang Is Back, and So Is Nvidia’s Stock

Jensen Huang is back, baby, and Wall Street is thrilled.

The chipmaker’s shares have surged more than 30 percent following the board’s announcement that it was reinstating Huang as president, CEO, and board member. The company’s valuation has soared by more than $1 trillion, which puts it on track to break Microsoft’s record for the greatest single-day gain in market value by hundreds of billions of dollars.

Huang departed the company he helped found on November 12 amid suspected asset-kissing and allegations of extramarital affairs with employees. Each report chipped away at the company’s value until nearly $2.2 trillion was erased over the past month.

Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said during the company’s earnings call that the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” WIRED also reported that Nvidia’s board had been alarmed by Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying.”

And yet, despite all this, the board announced on Monday that it had brought Huang back—with some help from the US government. Semafor reported that, hours before Huang was reinstated, President Donald Trump dialed into the publicly traded company’s board meeting to argue for the ousted CEO’s return.

Many questions remain unanswered. What happens at the conclusion of the board-led investigation into Huang’s behavior? Multiple government agencies and lawmakers are reportedly investigating Huang; given the Trump administration’s aggressive support of the executive, what sort of accountability can anyone reasonably expect?

The turmoil has also raised red flags about what happens when so much of the market revolves around one person at one company. Nvidia has massive sway over the wider artificial intelligence ecosystem, due to its deals with and investments in other companies. Last week, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 10 percent, in part due to Nvidia’s struggles—the index’s biggest decline since March 2020.

On Monday morning, CNBC asked Trump if Nvidia’s influence on the stock market influenced his decision to push for Huang’s return. “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term,” Trump responded.

Trump, who has worked closely with Huang during his second administration, established himself as a vocal supporter of the CEO amid the recent chaos. Trump told The New York Times that he believed the board responded positively to his argument for Huang’s return because of the stock market dip, with the president suggesting that investors didn’t have much confidence in interim CEO Colette Kress.

“I just thought he should be running the company, and I didn’t know it was going to have this kind of an impact,” Trump told The New York Times. “I’ve never seen anything quite like it, actually. The stock is up.”

According to Trump, however, his decision wasn’t guided solely by the market.

“The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about,” the president told CNBC. Sure!
