#520. Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?

In April, about 60 countries held an unprecedented meeting in Colombia to work out a plan to slowly quit oil, coal and gas. How influential is this coalition at the COP31 climate summit?

This time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal. More than 80 countries backed the idea.

But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.

As a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap. At the same time, a group of 57 countries frustrated with the deadlock at the consensus-based UN talks decided to form a "coalition of the willing" to accelerate the fossil fuel exit outside the COP framework.

They held their own summit in April in Santa Marta, Colombia — the first such conference to specifically focus on implementing the transition away from fossil fuels (referred to as TAFF).

Co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands, the Santa Marta conference brought together countries including Canada, Norway, Brazil, Nigeria, Mexico, Australia and Germany, as well as highly climate-vulnerable states such as Vanuatu.

The idea was for governments to start developing national roadmaps and working out how to restructure their financial and trade systems to wean themselves off polluting energy sources — an incredibly complicated undertaking, particularly for developing countries dependent on revenue from fossil fuel exports.

Part of their discussions focused on cutting subsidies for oil, coal and gas, as well as supporting people whose livelihoods rely on the fossil fuel industry to find new forms of income.

A little over six months on from the Santa Marta meeting, representatives from almost 200 countries are holding talks in Antalya, Turkey, as part of the latest UN climate conference.

Countries agreed for the first time in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels — the main driver behind rising global temperatures. But summits since then have failed to pin down how to implement that pledge.

It's not yet clear whether the Santa Marta coalition will influence ambition at this year's COP.

"I think it's more of a long-term game," said Chetna Hareesh Kumar, a climate policy analyst at the Berlin-based research organization NewClimate Institute.

She says it's too soon to expect the coalition to have an influence on the negotiations but adds that that could change at future COPs. The grouping could bring more nations on board if, for example, it shows it can be truly inclusive, address the needs of different types of countries and show that a transition is feasible.

One role the group is playing, according to Alexandra Scott, a senior climate diplomacy adviser at Italian climate change think tank ECCO, is "keeping up the political momentum," and showing "that there is this huge group of countries who really want to accelerate this transition away from fossil fuels."

She says it's also building an invaluable "cadre of knowledge" on how to develop national TAFF plans and deal with barriers individual countries face — like how to secure funding for the infrastructure investments needed for the energy transition.

The Santa Marta group is "really answering a lot of the questions that countries have always had on how on earth do we even start to transition our whole economy off fossil fuels?" Scott said.

This expertise being shared and tested in practice can show what such a transformation could look like and the knowledge brought into COP, added Scott.

Since the Santa Marta conference, Germany, France and the Netherlands have released national plans to phase out fossil fuels. While the plans contain no new commitments, experts see them as a positive first step.

Kumar says more countries could announce similar plans just ahead of the second TAFF summit in Tuvalu next year. Finland presented its TAFF roadmap in the first week of COP, but analysts do not expect many more countries to follow suit soon.

Another potential boost that could get momentum going is Brazil's recently published global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, promised at last year's COP.

The nearly 200-page document seeks to serve as a toolkit for countries shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy, such as wind and solar. It envisages countries making a phased transition between 2028 and 2033.

The aim, Ana Toni, CEO of last year's COP, told AP, is to break down the transition into "smaller actionable solutions" and help countries make practical progress.

The roadmap suggests measures tailored to each country's circumstances, including dependence on fossil fuel and financial capacities. "Levers" it proposes include reducing fossil fuel subsidies, expanding renewable energy and cutting methane emissions.

Kumar called it a "customizable" approach that allows every country to take action, regardless of its situation. "The question really is now what countries do with it and how much momentum they can generate," she added.

This year's climate change summit in Turkey — taking place after a series of deadly heat waves in Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people — isn't expected to result in any big announcements about fossil fuels.

Global renewable energy capacity has surged in recent years, making up a third of the world's power generation for the first time in 2025. But many countries still rely on coal, oil and gas.

A database compiled by the German environmental organization Urgewald shows that most oil and gas companies worldwide, among them QatarEnergy, Saudi Aramco and Russia's Gazprom, are exploring or developing new reserves.

Meanwhile, subsidies for fossil fuels amount to around $920 billion (around €830 billion) per year, according to data from the OECD, but that number is falling.

One issue Turkey is pushing at the COP conference is electrification. It's calling on countries to endorse the goal of 35% of final energy consumption coming from electricity by 2035 — up from around 20% today.

The pledge has drawn criticism from some circles, though, for leaving open whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources.

Ideally, Kumar said, electrification would be powered by renewables and tied to a goal of phasing out polluting fossil fuels.

"If something like that could make it to the final text, that would be a really good sign for momentum."

#517. The Feds Left Iowans in the Dark About Plans to Blow Up Tons of Lead

On October 26, Charles Massner, the mayor of Mediapolis, Iowa, got an email from the US Army. It described “an intentional, controlled detonation” of “a quantity of degraded lead azide … in the near future” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, some 20 miles south of Mediapolis.

The email, which was reviewed by WIRED, provided no details about when this explosion would happen, how much material the explosion would destroy, or what steps officials should take to protect the public from a possible toxic fallout. But it did request that public officials allow for environmental testing on public lands before and after the event, which the town granted in a November 2 meeting.

Massner says the next time he heard anything was early last week, when the Army published a press release on its website saying it would explode the lead azide in just a few days. That press release included a map of potential exposure from the blast. Mediapolis was directly in the path of exposure, covered in a reddish-yellow cloud with a hot pink border.

“There was really no communication, so to speak, other than what was on their website,” he says.

Massner wasn’t alone in being caught off guard. The sudden announcement that the Army would be exploding 9,500 pounds of lead azide with seemingly little to no notice caught nearly all of Iowa by surprise. Governor Kim Reynolds’ office said last week that they’d learned about the explosion the same way Massner did: via the press release sent out by the Army on November 15.

Now, despite a court order blocking the detonation, the Army announced late Sunday night that it plans to blow up the lead azide on Wednesday, a day before the Thanksgiving holiday. (On Monday, President Donald Trump posted that he was ordering the Army not to detonate anything without court approval.) Many Iowans are left with more questions than answers. Iowa’s unofficial state subreddit is filled with posts from people trying to plan holiday travel and safety around the event, which has switched dates twice in the past week. One local official in the path of a potential fallout told WIRED on Friday that she was leaving the area and staying at a hotel with her immunocompromised child.

Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the University of Iowa who has studied exposure to lead in his laboratory, says his lab has been “deluged with concerns,” with everyone from pediatricians to parents to people who run cleaning facilities and are worried about their staff exposure reaching out. Like most Iowans, Thorne also heard about the explosion from the Army’s press release.

“My first reaction was, They’re going to do what?” he says.

The 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at the Middletown site have been there for more than 20 years. In March, according to a document released by the Army on November 18, the material was officially labeled hazardous waste, and officials began looking into how to dispose of it. In a court filing published Saturday, the Army says that there is an “immediate risk” of the material exploding by itself after temperatures drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit. It is now invoking emergency powers to detonate the barrels by November 24.

“In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion,” the filing states.

The Army did not immediately respond to a list of questions sent by WIRED.

The Army does seem to have looked into other options besides blowing up the azide. The New York Times reported Friday that the Army awarded a contract in late March to a private company to handle cleaning up the chemicals onsite. However, that contract was pulled two months later; the company told the Times that the Army did not give a reason for changing its mind on the cleanup. A contracting officer in the Army told the company that the Army’s decision to pursue detonation “was not based on deficiencies” with the company’s science.

In a letter sent to Governor Reynolds on Friday, the EPA Region 7 administrator said that the agency only learned that the material had degraded to a dangerous state in March. The letter also listed a number of strategies the EPA had considered besides detonation, including chemical cleanup, which also risked causing an explosion.

The Army has blown up expired munitions before, although not at the scale of what it plans to do in Iowa. Thorne says that any exposure to lead from the explosion is expected to be “quite a bit lower” than lead exposures in communities exposed to legacy pollution sources. But “there is no safe level for lead, especially for young children,” he says.

The Army did have some public meetings and communications in late October with officials in Middletown, where the explosion will take place and where it has recommended temporary evacuation measures for some neighborhoods. But it’s not clear why its initial direct outreach around public health didn’t extend to towns in potential fallout ranges for a blast, including Mediapolis, beyond asking for permission to test soil samples. (The Army did include recommended public health measures in its November 15 press release.)

Thorne, a former chair of the EPA’s Science Advisory Board, says that a successful public health outreach program has lots of opportunity for public engagement for all affected areas.

“You have public meetings. You answer questions. You have extensive Q&A and FAQs, and you have people speaking to why this is the only choice, what are the burdens, and some kind of a cost-benefit comparison between the options, and then you roll it out through the media, through social media, through many ways,” he says. “Best practice is not what they’ve done—I think this is closer to worst practice, from a public health perspective.”

For his part, Massner, Mediapolis’s mayor, said on Friday that he planned to take “standard precautions” and follow the Army’s public health recommendations. (The Army has not released fallout modeling for a Wednesday explosion, but if winds carry the material south, it would be possible for Mediapolis to no longer be in the affected zone.) But Massner says he understands why people in his town were freaked out.

“What people saw was the map they drew, which showed a [red] cloud going over everybody’s head. I don’t think that was the intent of the map,” he laughs. “When you see a map covered in red, you’re supposed to run for shelter immediately—your life is in danger.”

Update: 11/23/2026, 2:01 PM EDT: WIRED has updated the piece to clarify that President Donald Trump said he will defer to an appeals court on whether the material will be detonated.

#514. Bobby Moynihan on Reggie Dinkins, his SNL return, and You Can See Everything

On Mashable's Say More, hosts Kristy Puchko (Mashable's Entertainment Editor) and Mark Stetson (Senior Creative Producer) bring humor and their trusted insights to the biggest shows, films, digital trends, and cultural moments. From viral-worthy rants and passionate raves to smart recaps and first-look teasers, they cover what everyone is talking about. Celebrity guests join the conversation for real talk about their careers, upcoming projects, and what’s trending online.

2026 has been a banner year for Bobby Moynihan. On top of returning to Saturday Night Live as Drunk Uncle and voicing characters in Grand Theft Auto VI and Pixar's Hoppers, he also plays a daffy sidekick to Tracy Morgan in NBC's exceptional comedy The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins.

Now in its second season, Reggie Dinkins follows a disgraced football player (Morgan) who invites a documentarian (Daniel Radcliffe) to stay with him and make a film that will rehabilitate his image. The growing relationship between the two oddly echoes the story at the heart of one of the year's buzziest titles: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything.

"When I saw the trailer for You Can See Everything, I went, 'That's our show,'" Moynihan told Mashable Entertainment Reporter Belen Edwards while he visited our Say More studio.

The connection between the documentary and the sitcom was so clear that a scene parodying the infamous "why would I deceive you?" exchange wound up in an episode of Reggie Dinkins that was scheduled for later in the season. However, since the episode would have aired far later than the trailer's initial release, the show's team worried the reference would feel too dated and removed it. Morgan, Radcliffe, and Moynihan shot the parody as promo for Season 2 instead, so it still saw the light of day.

"If I am being one billion percent honest, I don't know if Tracy knows who Elizabeth Holmes is right now, even after we've done it," Moynihan said. "We showed up, and he was like, 'What's this?' and we held up cue cards, and he was like, 'Never mind, I got it.'"

#510. Germany news: Merz, Söder aim to revisit electricity tax cut

The Christian Democrats are in Munich, pushing to revive some tax relief that didn't make it into the budget after talks last week. And Manuela Schwesig faces a vote on a new term as regional leader. Follow DW.

Stay tuned for more on these stories and anything else in or concerning Germany on November 16, 2026.

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow. Bis dann!

Germany dominated neighbor and historic rival the Netherlands in their Nations League quarterfinal match-up at Berlin's Olympic Stadium on Monday evening.

It was the team's sixth game under head coach Jürgen Klopp and the 50th ever between the two sides.

Germany's 5-0 shellacking of the Oranje was their most lopsided victory since 1959, when they won 7-0. In all, Germany have now won 19 of those matches, the Netherlands have won 12, and 18 ended in a draw.

Speaking to German broadcaster ARD after the game, attacking midfielder Florian Wirtz — who scored twice in the fixture — said: "We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second half."

Despite the loss, Xavi Hernandez's Dutch side will reach the final eight alongside Germany.

Prior to the match, Klopp had made it clear that he and his team were approaching Monday's showdown as a final after having lost to Greece 1-0 in his first home game in the job on September 27.

By night's end, Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck each scored once and Brajan Gruda scored once and added two assists on top of Wirtz's double.

Klopp has been high on Wirtz, who has come under fire for not delivering at Liverpool since his arrival there in June 2025, and his bet seems to be paying off with the 23-year-old now scoring four goals in his last four games for Germany.

"We don't care who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," said Wirtz on Monday evening before adding: "We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team."

A group of five EU member states, including Germany, have entered talks over a scheme to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

The plan to set up so-called return hubs in a non-EU country had been announced by the group — which also includes Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark — had first been announced back in September.

Tesla has earmarked some €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory in Germany, near to Berlin.

The Grünheide complex will be expanded to start producing the electric car company's driverless Cybercabs, with output expected to eventually reach 1 million units.

The Elon Musk-owned company said construction would begin in 2027, with the first Cybercabs rolling off the line in 2029.

"With this, we are laying the foundations for the world's most technologically advanced Tesla factory here in Grünheide," Tesla said.

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

Matt Pearson on our sports desk breaks down where the power struggle currently stands, with the deadline for candiates just a matter of hours away now.

Lawmakers in the state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have voted in Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier.

The 52-year-old has been in the role since 2017 and is heading into a third term.

The vote was a secret ballot, but it can still be assumed who voted and how.

She received 39 of the 68 votes cast in the chamber, exactly as many as commanded by Schwesig's three-party coaliton of her Social Democrats (29), the ecologist Greens (5), and the socialist Left Party (5).

While Söder's comments in Munich focused in particular on the policy the coalition in Berlin had not delivered, Merz initiatlly focused on talking up the efficacy of his federal coalition.

"We are aware of the situation. We know that we now need to deliver. And we also know that we face difficult talks within the coalition. But I would also say from the experiences of the last weeks that there are solutions to the problems which we have in Germany," Merz said.

Merz said that in the 18 months since last year's election, the coalition "has already successfully implemented many things, not 'set them into motion' as people like to say, but actually implemented."

He noted a total of 17 bills going through the second and third reading process in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, last week, "including the most comprehensive reforms of our intelligence and security services that we have ever done in [post-war] Germany."

Among others, he thanked Bavarian Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a senior member of the Bavarian CSU sister party to Merz's own conservative CDU, for his contribution to this.

Merz also touted the support given to CSU politician Ilse Aigner, not just from his CDU but from the Social Democrat coalition partners and the Greens, to become the next president, calling her a person who would "represent our country very well at home and abroad."

After hailing these accomplishments, Merz then turned to electricity tax cuts, saying he anticipated talks on the matter on Tuesday that would be "very short."

He said that over the weekend, coalition leaders had revisited the figures, and now believed they would be able to "completely" reduce electricity taxes to the minimum European levels in 2027 "also for private households."

Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has appeared with Friedrich Merz at a press conference during the chancellor's trip to Munich.

It seems Söder, Merz and the CDU/CSU believe they have unfinished business after the budget was finalized in the Bundestag late last week.

Merz had pledged in the run-up to the decision to provide a reduction in electricity tax for all, but the final agreement did not include this step, with the coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) saying it was not adequately costed.

Söder said he and Merz had discussed "backup for the coming days," for Berlin and for a "collective stance, that is really, really important."

He said the coming days were about "demonstrating credibility in politics," seemingly in reference to Merz's promise that the coalition did not ultimately deliver.

"That's why it's really important to us that we do indeed bring about the reduction in electricity tax," Söder said. "This is important for businesses. It would be a relief for citizens. But it's also a matter of credibility and it's written in the coalition agreement."

Söder said that as to the question of "where the money comes from, with a €560 billion (roughly $615 billion) budget, with €200 billion in new debt, nobody can tell me there's no potential within the budgeting process."

A festive piece of merchandise on the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) "fan shop" website has upset some religious leaders in Germany.

Called a "chocolate Nicholas," it appears to depict a semblance of Saint Nicholas in bishop's regalia and the party's colors and holding a book with "AfD" written on the cover where a Bible might be in more traditional iconography.

The Bishop of Essen, Franz-Josef Overbeck, was highly critical of the promotion in Monday's edition of the Bild newspaper.

"The AfD is appropriating Christian symbols for party campaigning," Overbeck said. "Showing the holy Nicholas in a blue coat with mitre, staff and the gospel with an AfD logo is not in order."

Overbeck acknowledged that other organizations like football clubs would sell chocolate Christmas figurines in club colors, but he said they would tend to refrain from including overtly Christian symbols when doing so.

Bild quoted an AfD spokesman as saying that as a "liberal-conservative party that clearly associates itself with Christian values," the item fit "particularly well" with the party image.

The main German protestant church group EKD's cultural representative, Johann Hinrich Claussen, said the offer showed the AfD had "no understanding of traditions and no respect" for Christianity.

He described the action as "embarrassing and revealing," and said that Christianity was "supra-partisan."

"The AfD knows little about what is holy to Christians. Otherwise, it would be aware that Bishop Nicholas of Myra, in what today is Demre in Turkey, stood clearly for uniting the occident and the orient. Beyond that, he is the patron saint of rescues at sea," Claussen said.

The partner of deceased Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger has said that anybody is welcome at his funeral this coming Saturday.

Aiwanger was the economy minister in Bavaria's state government as the leader of the junior coalition partners to the center-right CSU.

"Hubert was a man of the people and so it stands to reason that anyone who liked or treaasured him is allowed to come to his funeral," Tanja Schweiger wrote on her Instagram profile overnight.

She was posting after a requiem in the state capital Munich paying tribute to the leader of the Free Voters (Freie Wähler) party over the weekend. Around 1,100 people attended this ceremony.

Aiwanger died suddenly and unexpectedly on November 4 during a working visit to Berlin, aged 55.

Prosecutors have since said he died of natural causes, after he was found dead in his hotel room.

Germany's national men's football team will play neighbors and rivals the Netherlands for the 50th time on Monday night.

And there's quite a lot at stake for Jürgen Klopp's team in the last group stage game of the Nations League competition at Berlin's Olympiastadion.

If Germany win, they will qualify for the knockout stages, but a defeat could lead to potential relegation into the second tier of Nations League football.

Klopp was upbeat in the pre-match press conference at the prospect of playing the Netherlands, who he said play "Xavi football," in the image of the skillful Spanish playmaker and World Cup winner coaching the team.

"I've always loved playing against teams like this. For all my coaching career," Klopp said. "When someone says, 'hey they can really play football,' then in my mind the party's already started."

A full house with some 71,000 fans is expected in the capital when the game kicks off. Klopp played on the Dutch reputation for liberal use of bicylces in his comments to reporters, saying he wanted to "put a stick in their spokes" and dislodge them from the saddle.

The notion of a bridge over the valley between Ratingen and Heiligenhaus to the east of Düsseldorf in western Germany as part of the A44 highway is more than half a century old. And the physical bridge itself has stood, complete, ever since 2022.

Yet still the crossing is not connected to any roads at either end.

A construction project to build the last 4.4 kilometers of highway and link the bridge to the A44 highway will formally start on Monday.

State premier Hendrik Wüst, as well as the regional transport and traffic ministers will attend the ground-breaking ceremony.

A project first conceived some 55 years ago has faced repeated delays because of lawsuits, environmental protection studies and onerous planning and permit procedures.

The bridge across the Angerbachtal (Angerbach Valley) should improve the road connection between the North Rhine-Westphalia state capital of Düsseldorf, the Bergisches Land mountain range and the industrial cities in the Ruhr Valley. It's also meant to help remove some strain from the perenially busy A3 highway and to improve the road connections to Düsseldorf International Airport.

The last stretch of highway is expected to cost around €200 million (roughly $220 million), or roughly the annual costs incurred each year by forcing traffic to divert around it, according to estimates from Düsseldorf's IHK industry and trade association.

Construction is expected to take several years, no formal end date has yet been set.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz heads to Munich early on Monday, for a meeting with the leadership of the Bavarian Christian Social Democrats (CSU), the sister party to his conservative  Christian Democrats(CDU).

No concrete details about the talks were made public ahead of time, except for the CSU saying it would serve as a general exchange that had been planned for some time.

The trip comes a week after Merz nominated Ilse Aigner as the next German president, likely paving the way for her to become the first woman and first CSU politician to assume the role.

It also follows soon after the 2027 federal budget cleared a marathon meeting of the parliamentary budget committee in Berlin. This serves as one of the more conspicuous examples of the frictions and difficulties in the grand coalition between the Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats — with the compromises it contains a point of frustration among the CSU and for state premier Markus Söder.

The northeastern state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will likely vote in Social Democrat (SPD) Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier early in the afternoon.

The 52-year-old, who first stepped into the role in 2017, plans to lead a new coalition of the SPD, the environmentalist Greens and the socialist Left Party after state elections in September.

The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the largest single party in the sparsely populated state.

But still, the political calculus that emerged was arguably simpler than in Berlin — where the socialist Left Party is the largest party but could struggle to lead a coaltion — and in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD was by far the largest party but short of an outright majority.

Schwesig's SPD claimed 29 seats, with the Greens and the Left each taking 5, meaning that when combined, they hold a fairly clear majority over the AfD with its 32 seats.

The SPD's relatively successful performance in the state, at least compared to its national struggles, has also led to Schwesig being linked with a possible return to federal politics. The SPD plans to elect a new leadership duo early next year.

Schwesig has already had a spell in Berlin as the federal minsiter for families, pensioners and women, and briefly led the SPD on an interim basis in 2017, but after this she returned to her home state to seek the top regional job instead.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Servus! Welcome to another Monday of news and analysis of matters making waves in German politics and society.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is starting his week in Munich, at a meeting of the Bavarian CSU sister party to his conservative Christian Democrats (CDU).

This comes a few days after Merz naming CSU politician Ilse Aigner as candidate to be the next president, and days after the budget committee signed off on the federal government's spending plans for 2027. Merz is expected to appear with state premier Markus Söder in a joint press conference later.

Far to the north, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Social Democrat Manuela Schwesig should be voted in for another term as state premier in the regional parliament later in the day. Schwesig emerged in pole position after state elections a few weeks ago; some suspect her regional success could translate into national ambitions within the struggling party.

And in the west, regional leaders are headed to a road to nowhere — literally, but also hopefully not for very much longer now.

The vast highway A44 bridge over the valley between Helsinghausen and Ratingen-Ost has been planned for decades, and was completed in 2022, but work to actually connect it to the road network will only start today.

Stay with us for more on these stories and whatever else develops around Germany on November 16.

#508. How to Win Big Betting on Jensen Huang? Listen to Trump

Just days ago, Jensen Huang’s chances of returning as Nvidia CEO looked increasingly slim, at least according to prediction markets. Earlier this month, Huang resigned from the AI hardware giant following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence services. As more reports emerged about Huang’s alleged bad behavior, Nvidia’s board insisted it had no plans to reinstate him. By early Sunday morning on the East Coast, traders on Polymarket’s US platform put his chances of returning at just 10 percent. But by Monday, Huang was back in charge.

The swings in Huang’s odds on prediction markets offer a window into how his unlikely comeback unfolded and who saw it coming. The New York Times reported that President Trump played a crucial role in convincing the board to bring Huang back. Traders who paid attention to what Trump and his allies wanted appear to have fared much better than those who did not.

On Sunday evening in Washington, Huang’s odds on Polymarket US jumped 6 percentage points in just 40 minutes after Trump published a Truth Social missive calling for Huang’s reinstatement. The president said he wanted to help revive the stock market, which had plunged following Huang’s scandal, a sign of Nvidia’s enormous influence over the AI industry and broader US economy.

According to the prediction market intelligence firm Betting Intelligence, the odds on both Kalshi and Polymarket largely tracked with public signals about the likelihood of Huang’s return. They rose when Huang said he was open to coming back, fell when the board dismissed the possibility, and climbed again when Trump threw his support behind the former CEO.

But Betting Intelligence and the prediction market forensics firm MSR Decode also identified clusters of trades that did not appear to be driven by news or public commentary. Kalshi and Polymarket declined to comment on whether they are currently investigating potential insider trading in markets related to Huang’s return.

Despite these anomalies, Betting Intelligence CEO Dan Zimmermann says the Huang-related markets showed fewer signs of potentially suspicious activity than usual. “The group that could have known the board’s decision in advance was small. So the market was mostly headline chasers and long-shot buyers,” he says.

For traders who profited from Huang’s comeback, the lesson is clear: Don’t discount Trump.

Isaac Rose-Berman, a research and policy fellow at the American Institute for Boys & Men and a professional sports bettor, says he made approximately $10,000 wagering on Huang’s return on Kalshi. He placed his trade after the Nvidia chief said on X that he was open to reclaiming his old job. Rose-Berman says he figured that people like Trump, who had an interest in boosting Nvidia’s stock price, would successfully pressure the board to reinstate Huang. (Never mind the concerns about national security or Huang allegedly threatening employees that he would “pee in your brain.”)

“It’s 2026 and Trump is president, scandal schmandal,” Rose-Berman says. “Should’ve bet more.”

A pseudonymous prediction market trader known as Domer tells WIRED he cleared approximately $600,000 by placing an early wager last week on Huang’s return. He wasn’t focused explicitly on Trump’s desires, but he says his understanding of power dynamics ultimately guided his approach. “Boards can be very malleable,” he tells WIRED.

Other prediction market “sharps” say that commentary from Trumpworld was the strongest signal available about Huang’s return. As some bettors noted, there was a notable opportunity for profit after Trump suggested to a PBS NewsHour reporter that Huang would be back in power soon, but before Nvidia officially announced his reinstatement. “The key was looking at Trump’s support and the recent performance of the stock market,” says Kalshi trader Caleb Davies.

Aaron Courtney, a data analyst and cofounder of a prediction market analytics firm, says he took a loss on his Huang position. Looking back, he says his mistake was not paying attention to what Trump and other administration officials said over the weekend. “Trump saying he hoped Nvidia would bring Jensen back would be the clearest signal,” he says.

Update 11/23/26 9:05 pm ET: This story has been updated to clarify Isaac Rose-Berman’s reasoning for wagering on Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO.

#506. The best wireless earbuds weve ever tested (and continue to love)

If you're looking for a new pair of earbuds, we have good news: You have a lot of options. The bad news? You have a lot of options, and your decision can get overwhelming, fast. Wasn't life easier when iPhones came with a free pair of earbuds?

While you can still find wired earbuds that plug in and go, the market is flooded with high-quality wireless options. Now, you'll find models with advanced active noise cancellation, multi-point pairing, high-resolution audio support, and extra-long battery life. To help you choose, Mashable's audio experts put the best wireless earbuds from Apple, Bose, Sony, and other top brands to the test.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

The best wireless earbuds range anywhere from $10 to $1,000, especially if you're going for professional-grade studio earphones. And if you care about active noise cancellation, you can easily spend $300 — that's the price of peace and quiet. You can also get hyperspecialized models like sleep earbuds, bone-conduction earbuds for working out, and open earbuds for transparency. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

In 2026, our top picks for earbuds are the Sony WF-1000XM6, Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd gen), and Panasonic Technics AZ100s, which provide outstanding sound quality and ANC. But keep in mind that these models will run you $299 to $329. While we stand by the value of everything on this list, we know that spending over $300 on a pair of earbuds is a lot to stomach. That's why we've also included more budget-friendly wireless earbuds under $100 that still deliver excellent performance.

Ready to start shopping now? Here are our favorite wireless and noise-cancelling earbuds as of November 2026.

Read our full review of the Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds.

Anyone looking for the all-around best experience: Sony's new XM6 earbuds are the follow-up we've been waiting for from the brand. Though they cost a lot, they justify their price point in an excellent performance on all fronts, which brings some of the best ANC, sound quality, design, and ease of use to one elegant package.

Sony built a reputation for providing some of the best sound quality available in the game, and while we still think the Technics on this list eke out a better performance, Sony's overall package is unrivaled.

The earbuds sound great out of the box, but the 10-band equalizer gives the user plenty of options for customization. Whether we listened to classic rock or straight-up classical concertos, these earbuds made music sound immersive, rich, and clear. To supplement the great sound quality, Sony also stepped up its ANC game from the previous gen, resulting in the best ANC we've ever encountered on a pair of earbuds. Though we wish it were adjustable (especially at this price point), if you're looking to block out the world around you as much as possible, we think these perform even better than our former favorites, the Bose QC Ultra 2 buds.

Where Bose has Sony beat is in comfort. Sony did redesign the shape of its earbuds from the previous gen, helping provide an even more comfortable and flush fit. Still, Bose's stability band still takes the cake for the best fit we've ever experienced — but Sony is closing that comfort gap.

Read our full review of the Panasonic Technics EAH-AZ100 earbuds.

Audiophiles first and foremost: If you want to hear every note in perfect crisp detailed sound, the Panasonic's Technics EAH-AZ100 make music better thanks to their magnetic fluid drivers. Whether you want a fully customizable experience by adjusting your bass and treble, or you just want to pop in your buds and experience delicious spatial audio without the fuss, the Technics offer users both.

Panasonic blew us away with its Technics EAH-AZ100 earbuds. If you've ever thought that earbuds can't deliver the same potent sound quality as over-ear headphones, then let the AZ100s prove you wrong. The buds come with four different ear tips that range from extra small to large, delivering a snug and secure fit suitable for even those with small or narrow ears who struggle to find earbuds that fit. That being said, they aren't the most comfortable headphones we've ever tested (nothing beats the Bose QuietComfort Ultras), as they get uncomfortable after a couple of hours of wear.

However, what you're really after here is the incredible sound quality of the Technics. Music just sounds better on the AZ100 earbuds. The earbuds deliver music as close to the source as possible. While listening to James Brown's "The Boss," the song sounded rich and textured, with layers of horn and deep bass bursting through. Plus, it picks up on the most subtle details, like in "Angel Of My Dreams" by Jade, the soft shuttering of cameras flashing on the backing track rang through in crisp detail.

Plus, these headphones have impressive active noise cancellation. While testing them on a trip to New York, they blocked out the clatter of the subway and ruckus of noisy streets. With such excellent ANC, nothing distracts from the superior audio quality. The three-way multipoint connection is another huge advantage of these headphones. I could seamlessly switch between my iPhone, iPad, and MacBook Pro without having to open the app.

Not to mention, these earbuds have killer battery life. They last for 10 hours with an additional 28 hours available with the charging case.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra earbuds (2nd gen).

Long-haul travelers, students, or anyone who can't get earbuds to fit quite right: For those who value noise cancellation and all-day wear above all else, the $299 Bose QuietComfort Ultra earbuds (2nd gen) are worth the investment. With spatial audio and some of the best ANC we've encountered, these earbuds deliver immersive sound that envelopes you in your music.

Over-ear headphones are the typical pick for those who want the best noise cancellation, but these days, you're no longer limited if you prefer earbuds but still want top-tier ANC.

Bose's second iteration of its QuietComfort Ultra earbuds doesn't change too much from the original, with the main improvements coming in the form of wireless charging, improved speech clarity on calls, and better adaptive ANC, but we also noticed some minor improvements to the sound profile, which also did a great job of sounding full and resonant right out of the box.

Where these earbuds really shine, however, is in their name: it's their fit and noise cancellation. Though they only have three sizes of ear tips and stability bands, the design of these earbuds allows for a fit that's both secure and comfortable enough to wear for hours on end, which isn't a given with earbuds. The noise cancellation impresses, too, even without any music playing, thanks to the eight microphones packed into these buds. Common household sounds like air conditioning, neighbors, and other people existing in your space all but disappear with the ANC bumped all the way up. If you don't like that much blockage, you can turn on transparency mode or manually adjust the level of ANC.

So what are the downsides? Besides being priced like a premium pair of earbuds (which, to be fair, they are in their performance), the six-hour battery life is starting to lag behind competitors. Plus, the equalizer is less sophisticated than what you'll find on other earbuds, and the touch controls weren't quite as seamless as we want on $300 earbuds. Still, for the combo of noise-cancelling and comfort, we can't choose a better pair of earbuds.

Read our full review of the Apple AirPods Pro 3.

Apple fans: Apple device owners will appreciate how easily these earbuds pair with multiple devices, as well as their impressive active noise cancellation and the many ways they can be used.

The AirPods Pro pop up on most best of lists, and though we've always been fans, the third generation takes these earbuds to a new level.

At the most basic level, these earbuds perform well in all the ways you'd want them to: the sound profile is robust and clear, the noise cancellation truly silences the world around you, and they pair easily to Apple devices. With this generation, Apple bumped up these buds' battery life to eight hours per charge, putting them firmly on the higher end of what's available on the market.

Then, there are the extra features. Apple included a built-in heart rate monitor, which can be used when you track your workouts with the Fitness app. How did it perform? "Perfectly," according to Mashable contributor Adam Doud's review. "I checked the heart rate against another device...and in every instance, the heart rate from the AirPods Pro 3 was within a beat or two per minute of the other device, so that speaks very well for its accuracy." Along with the IP57 water- and sweat-resistance and five sizes of ear tips for finding just the right fit, the AirPods Pro have become a much better pair of earbuds for working out this generation.

Finally, the live translation. At the time of writing, it's available in English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and English from the UK. Doud wrote that it worked fairly accurately (as compared to movie subtitles) with a one to two second delay, making the feature viable for real-time use.

At $249, the Apple AirPods Pro 3 are on par (and even cheaper) than other premium competitors. So what's the catch? Well, for anyone looking to fine-tune their own audio experience, there's no companion app or custom equalizer, but for everything else you get, the trade-off may well be worth it.

Read our full review of the AirPods 5 with wireless charging case.

Apple fans on a budget: The AirPods Pro 3 are great, but with the addition of better noise cancellation, a wireless charging case, volume controls on the stem, and live translation to the AirPods 5 model, you can get a very similar experience for $100 cheaper, making this the best value option for Apple-centric users.

These are also a great pick for anyone who wants earbuds that sit in between an in-ear and open earbud, as they don't have an ear tip that's situated in the ear canal, but rather rest near it as a traditional earbud would.

Apple pulled a rare move by lowering the prices on the AirPods 5 while adding more features, which made our job pretty easy in recommending them. They come with 50 percent better ANC than the AirPods 4, while being $149 compared to the 4's $179. Despite being a semi-in-ear model, they provide a surprising amount of sound control. Mashable Senior Editor Stan Schroeder wrote in his review that though they struggled on higher-pitched sounds, "on an actual plane, I realized they did a pretty good job of reducing both the engines' drone and the passengers' chatter."

He was also particularly impressed by how they sounded for live performances, as open earbuds tend to let the wider soundstage shine more than traditional in-ear buds, which might emphasize clarity and bass — he appreciated the width of the sound. These earbuds also come with the Live Translation feature found on the AirPods Pro 3, which allows for language translation in real time, as well as a volume sliding control on the stem. You'll miss out on the more expensive earbuds' built-in heart rate monitor and Hearing Protection feature, but if neither is too important to you, you'd likely be better off saving the cash. The biggest difference besides the wear is perhaps the battery life: where the AirPods Pro 3 get eight hours per charge, you'll have to settle for five hours per charge with the AirPods 5, but you will have a smaller carrying case than the Pros.

Bargain hunters: Finding a solid pair of budget earbuds is all about balance, and the EarFun Air Pro 4 exemplify that perfectly. While not the absolute cheapest pair of earbuds you could buy, they're still less than $100 and perform at the level of earbuds double their price. For anyone looking for the best value noise-cancelling earbuds, these are our top pick.

The EarFun earbuds don't fall into the pitfalls of other budget buds on the market. Yeah, you'll pay more than $50 pair (but only slightly if you grab them during one of their frequent sales). What you'll get in return is affordable earbuds that can adeptly handle a multipoint connection, feature a well-rounded sound profile with variation thanks to the in-app equalizer, and a battery life that can likely power you through most, if not all, of your workday.

The efficacy of the active noise cancellation is an especially standout feature of these earbuds, thanks to the absence noise breakthrough or strong hissing to supplement the power of the ANC. (Usually, one or both can be found on cheaper earbuds.) EarFun could've stopped there, but these earbuds also offer manually adjustable ANC, which isn't even a given on premium noise-cancelling earbuds. While not every level of adjustment is worth writing home about, it's still a nice addition.

Five sizes of ear tips ranging from XS to XL help with a comfortable fit and providing the best passive noise cancellation possible. Overall, these earbuds start to verge on too good to be true for their price point. The one major flaw we could find is that their on-ear touch controls verged on being both under-and overly sensitive, causing our tester to prefer toggling them off entirely in the companion app. Still, if there was one feature EarFun was going to flop on, this is maybe the least annoying of the bunch.

Read our full review of the Soundcore Sleep A30 Special earbuds.

Restless sleepers in noisy nighttime environments: Within a few months, Soundcore turned around and upgraded its already excellent Sleep A30 earbuds, bringing the Sleep A30 Special earbuds to the scene. For anyone who needs noise cancellation to help them get to sleep, the Sleep A30 Specials are basically your only option — thankfully, they're also one of the best valued options.

The major names in the sleep earbuds space are Ozlo and Soundcore. While Ozlo is known for being made by former Bose engineers, the $349 earbuds come at a huge price point — especially considering their lack of features in comparison to Soundcore's offerings.

Most notably, the Soundcore Sleep A30 Special earbuds offer active noise cancellation, the only sleep earbuds to do that other than their predecessor, the Sleep A30 earbuds. Even better, they do it at a significantly lower price point than the Ozlo buds at $229.99. While it's still a decent price to pay for earbuds solely designed for sleep, relatively speaking, A30 Specials offer some of the best value by far due to the feature set.

In addition to the ANC, the companion app offers several white noise options, including customizable soundscapes and Calm app meditations. If you prefer to stream your own audio, Soundcore's Bluetooth streaming with ANC on can last through an entire night of sleep (an upgrade from the regular A30 earbuds). The brand also recently added an update to the app that allows users to toggle on a timed turn-off for their audio, instead of the sleep detection option that existed at the earbuds' release.

These earbuds' case also monitors the environment in real time to provide adaptive snore masking, should the user toggle that option on. Standard features that exist on other earbuds will also be found on these buds, including a built-in alarm, sleep tracking data, and touch controls.

Read our full review of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 earbuds.

Runners, gym rats, and fitness fans: If you don't want to be bothered by loose or ill-fitting headphones while lifting or on a run, go for a pair that won't budge. The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 fit snuggly within the ear, but the extra ear hook adds an extra level of security. For iOS users, these connect instantly, but even Android users can benefit from a quick Bluetooth connection, too.

When you're on the go and want to stay hands-free, the Powerbeats Pro 2 have external controls for answering calls or playing music. Plus, the Powerbeats bring crisp sound that helps you block out sound when you'd rather focus on your workout and not the gym crowd around you. Not to mention, the Powerbeats also include a heart rate monitor for real-time readings.

The Powerbeats Pro have earned a permanent spot in my gym bag. They fit snuggly within the ear and with the ear hooks don't budge, no matter how sweaty I get or how I move through my workouts. As an iPhone user, they're a dream to connect, automatically doing so whenever I take them out of the case.

With their noise-cancelling capabilities, they're able to block out the noise of the gym or the outdoors. But if you want to be able to hear the world around you for safety, you can swap into Transparency Mode. The sound is clear and consistent. Is it the best sound quality I've tested? No, but it's still pretty great.

The on-ear earbud controls are great. The Beats Fit Pro suffered from overly sensitive controls, causing me to accidentally end a call or two. But the controls on the Powerbeats Pro 2 don't get set off by accidentally brushing them. The battery life on the Powerbeats Pro 2 is incredible, up to 45 hours with the case. I think I went a full month without charging them — even with daily use.

It actually wasn't love at first wear with the Powerbeats. At first, they're pretty awkward figuring out how to fit the bud in your ear and then hooking them around. Both my colleague, Bethany Allard, and I tested the Powerbeats and struggled with the learning curve of getting them to fit, and it was a bad first impression of the Beats. While I do like how customizable they are with five different ear tips, navigating their fit is difficult at first.

However, after a few months of use, I realized the Powerbeats Pro 2 became my go-to gym earbud. While other earbuds didn't sound as good, started to slip out when things got sweaty, or required frequent charging, I always returned to the Powerbeats Pro 2.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort earbuds.

Anyone who wants budget-friendly from a premium brand: If you want good-quality sound but don’t want to spend over $200, the Bose QuietComfort is an affordable answer to the brand’s lineup. They’re focused on a great fit, as they not only come with multiple ear tips but multiple bands that can be changed out on the earbuds for a better fit on the crest of your ear.

The accompanying app lets you adjust audio levels, but you won’t need to, as these earbuds make all your music sound better. They’re reliable, have a long battery life, and are sure to please the pickiest of audiophiles.

I’ve sung the praises of the QuietComfort Ultra, but Bose’s latest earbuds, the entry-level QuietComfort, are also fantastic, especially with their under-$200 price tag. Even after adjusting the ear tips and bands, I didn’t find the fit on these quite as secure as the Ultras. However, my colleague Bethany Allard, who also tested the QuietComfort earbuds, said they were the best earbuds that have ever fit her.

The QuietComfort’s sound quality is just phenomenal. With these earbuds, listening to Ethel Cain’s A House in Nebraska immersed me in the orchestrations. When Brick House by The Commodores came on, the earbuds elevated the snappy drum beats so that I may have been listening live.

The noise cancellation on the QuietComfort earbuds isn’t as sophisticated as the Ultras; I found they had more sound leakage and that classic ANC buzz when I was in noisy environments. However, the ANC on these is still great, especially in quiet spaces.

One tiny beef I have with the Bose QuietComfort earbuds is that they require a different app than the standard Bose one. This is annoying if you’re an existing Bose user and need to download another app; plus, this earbud app just isn’t as good as Bose’s flagship app.

All in all, these are a solid pair of headphones that, for $179, are an unbeatable value.

Read our full review of the Bose Ultra Open (2nd gen).

Anyone who finds earbuds too uncomfortable: If you want a pair of everyday earbuds with an open design, the latest Bose Ultra Open earbuds will be your best bet. Yes, $300 is a hefty investment, but they have the best sound quality of any open earbuds we've tried. Plus, Bose's clip-on design can't be beat, from the comfort to the colorways.

The open earbuds trend has taken off in the past few years for anyone who craves some more awareness when listening to their audio. Maybe it's because you don't want to totally feel siloed in your own world; maybe it's convenient for exercise, more comfortable, or simply safer with their heightened awareness. Whatever your reason for wearing them, in our testing, we found the second-generation Bose Ultra Open earbuds are the best choice for most folks.

We were already fans of the sound quality of the first-generation Bose open buds, but the second generation adds more bass and depth, making it the superior open earbud listening experience. Bose also nails the design. The clip is secure, easy to adjust, and comfortable enough to wear for hours. You'd think at least one of those areas would suffer, but Bose strikes the balance. Rounding out the top-tier design are the excellent color selection (black, white smoke, limited-edition cherry chocolate, olive green, and sky pink) and the best tactile controls you'll find on any pair of earbuds, thanks to the button on the top of the clip mechanism's back side. These buds also come with an IPX4 water and sweat resistance rating, so you're cleared for workouts.

So what's the catch? Well, they're expensive as hell, even for regular noise-cancelling earbuds. If these lean too pricey, our former top pick, the Shokz OpenDots One, is still a worthwhile (and more affordable) choice for clip-on earbuds.

Read our full review of the Soundcore AeroFit 2 Pro.

Versatility is key: The Soundcore AeroFit 2 Pro are the jack of all (earbud) trades, master of none. They're the only real option if you want to keep open and noise cancelling earbuds with you on the go without carrying around, or paying or, two completely separate pairs of earbuds. They're not the best in either department, but they're pretty solid in both, making them an excellent option for those who value convenience above all else.

Admittedly, the pool of options is pretty much limited to the AeroFit 2 Pro when considering dual-form earbuds — unless you count the noise-reduction features on Shokz OpenFit Pro. For true noise cancellation and open form wear however, you'll have to look to the Soundcore buds.

That criteria on its own doesn't earn these earbuds a spot on our list, though. Soundcore followed through on their innovative design by producing earbuds that actually perform well, too, even with their flaws. Let's start with the weakest point: these earbuds don't come with interchangeable ear tips (á la the AirPods 4), instead staying in place with an adjustable ear hook that looks them into the noise cancelling or open mode. While still relatively comfortable, it does mean that they suffer somewhat on the passive noise cancellation front. Paired with just-okay ANC, you won't be getting the best noise blocking out there — expect to be able to somewhat make out conversations of coworkers or fellow cafe-goers, though both will be dampened.

Still, if the best ANC isn't a top priority, this a fairly easy feature to overlook. Especially when a quick adjustment of the ear hook, you suddenly have the best transparency mode possible — an open-ear design. Soundcore has plenty of experience making solid open earbuds, so it came as no surprise that the sound on these was clear, relatively robust, and noticeably varied, especially with equalizer adjustments. The ear hook kept them sturdy and in place, making these IP55 dust and water-resistance rated buds an excellent option for wear while working out or simply staying aware while out and about.

There are two overarching types of earbuds: wireless and wired. While those descriptors are self-explanatory, let's get into the specifics of both.

Wireless earbuds connect to devices via Bluetooth for cordless usage. These earbuds range from $20 budget models to high-end models with active noise cancellation. While they don't require a wire to connect to a device, some wireless earbuds still have a wire that might go around the back of the neck to connect the buds.

While earbuds traditionally don't provide the passive noise cancellation of over-the-ear headphones, wireless models often feature ANC, which electronically blocks out background noise. With wireless headphones, you need to consider the battery life. Most models should have an eight-hour or more battery life before they need to be recharged.

Wired earbuds are the original model: two buds connected by a wire to your audio source. While they once felt high-tech, they're pretty basic now. Wired earbuds with active noise cancellation are basically non-existent, other than Bose's newest release.

The biggest positive of wired headphones is that they don't need to be charged. They're a great backup option to keep in your bag in case your usual wireless headphones or earbuds run out of charge.

We added the new Apple AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case to this guide in October following their September 2026 release as a cheaper alternative for Apple users, or for folks who don't prefer the ear tip fit of the AirPods Pro 3.

After extensive testing, Mashable Lead Shopping Reporter Bethany Allard rounded up the best sleep earbuds. You can read her full guide, but as of February 2026, we've added the Anker Soundcore Sleep A30 Special to this guide, which Allard says are the best sleep earbuds for most people. Also in February 2026, we added the Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds as our top pick for the best overall earbud, and removed the previous generation, the WF-1000XM5, as the best Sony earbud.

Bose recently announced two new open earbuds: the Ultra Open (2nd gen) and Sport Open. We'll be testing them out to see how they compare to the Shokz earbuds in this guide. Bose also released a new pair of wired noise-cancelling earbuds, which are a breakthrough in the wired earbuds market.

With the announcement that Bose is acquiring Skullcandy and the release of the Noise Master Buds Open earbuds with Sound by Bose, we'll be testing more Bose-powered audio products not directly from the brand.

If you're just looking for a pair of everyday wireless earbuds, all but one of the models in this guide will check that box. (We formerly included the Marshall Mode earbuds for folks who preferred a wired option, but have since removed them from our guide as the version we tested is difficult to find in stock these days.)

If you're looking for the highest quality wireless earbuds, you can't go wrong with the Sony WF-1000XM6, Bose QuietComfort Ultra, Apple AirPods Pro 3, and Panasonic Technics EAH-AZ100 earbuds, our most recent recommendations in 2026. All of these wireless earbuds feature elite noise cancellation, stellar sound, long battery life, and a comfortable fit for extended wear.

Though most earbuds are now wireless, this ultimately comes down to preference. If you have a tighter budget or don't want to worry about the battery running low all the time, wired earbuds are a great option. With that said, it is significantly harder to find wired earbuds with active noise cancellation. At the time of writing, the only pair with both wired connectivity and ANC both is from Bose — we're still in the process of testing them out.

To help you decide, we put a range of wireless earbuds to the test to determine which are worth your money. Whether you're simply looking for earbuds to get you through the work day, a pair to take with you on a flight, or a pair that you can live in 24/7, we have a set of buds for you. And if nothing on this list stands out to you, you can always expand your search to headphones as well.

As long as they're Bluetooth-compatible, these earbuds should connect to any smartphone, tablet, or laptop regardless of operating system. All of the earbuds on this list work equally well across iOS and Android systems with one exception — Apple AirPods.

Our favorite AirPods, the Apple AirPods Pro 3 are great and will connect to an Android device, but you won't get the same ease of connectivity or full array of features. However, other earbuds like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra earbuds and the Panasonic Technics AZ100 feature Android apps so you can experience their full range of features on an Android device.

Each pair of earbuds selected for this guide was hands-on tested by a Mashable reporter, editor, or contributor. Along with wireless earbuds tested specifically for this article, we also combed through our existing reviews to pick the best of the best earbuds for 2026. In addition to the bang for your buck, when testing earbuds, we consider criteria such as:

For each of our earbuds, we do our best to run their battery life out and test it against the stated battery life. All ANC earbuds are used with ANC, and while each tester defers to their preferred volume, we do try to average around the 50% mark when in use.

We tested out these earbuds with a variety of songs, from live performances to bass-heavy electronic music, R&B, rock, and folksy guitar songs. We evaluated how they sounded out of the box, along with any EQ presets or custom controls. Realistically, you'll make calls when using your earbuds, which is why we put each of these earbuds through a call test, making sure the person on the other end of the phone could hear us clearly and consistently.

Though this category can be subjective, we made sure each of our selections at least had several different ear tip sizes and were comfortable to wear for stretches of three hours or more. We also evaluate features like cleverly placed touch controls and stabilizers for keeping earbuds in place, both during casual use and exercise.

Any feature that made the earbuds stand out and also performed consistently well earned points in this category. For example, in addition to a rich out-of-the box sound profile, the Sony earbuds had an incredibly customizable and user-friendly experience with the in-app equalizer.

Bethany Allard is a Los Angeles-based shopping reporter at Mashable covering beauty tech, dating, sex and relationships, and headphones. That basically means she puts her hair through a lot, scrolls through a lot of dating apps, and rotates through a lot of different headphones. In addition to testing out and rounding up the best products, she also covers deals for Mashable, paying an especially obsessive amount of attention to Apple deals and prices. That knowledge comes in handy when she's covering shopping holidays like Prime Day and Black Friday, which she's now done for five years at Mashable.

Samantha Mangino, is an e-reader expert. She's tested all the Kindle and Kobo e-readers, diving into the buzziest models. Her love of reading extends beyond the e-reader beat, covering books and authors, too. In the tech space, she covers tablets, smart rings, and headphones.

#502. Starbucks just unveiled a limited-edition FriendsWithYou merch collection — how to buy

Starbucks has been incredibly busy lately. Between launching an incredibly cute Winnie the Pooh collection and all their holiday drops going live, they have somehow found the time to launch an ultra-colorful artist collaboration.

Starbucks is teaming up with Los Angeles-based art duo FriendsWithYou (Samuel Borkson and Arturo Sandoval III) on a limited-edition, six-piece drinkware collection arriving at select U.S. and Canadian locations from Nov. 24, while supplies last. Built around the duo’s signature Little Cloud Boy character and his new barista sidekick, Fluffy, the lineup spans ceramic mugs, insulated tumblers, and charm-adorned bottles.

There's a lot to like about this latest collection:

FriendsWithYou Ceramic Mug 16 oz — White and teal ceramic mug featuring a 3D Little Cloud Boy figurine perched on the handle ($24.95).

FriendsWithYou Cold Cup 24 oz — Plastic iced venti cup topped with Fluffy and Little Cloud Boy straw toppers ($29.95).

FriendsWithYou Glass Bottle 24 oz — Glass water bottle wrapped in a protective blue silicone sleeve with dangling FriendsWithYou character charms ($29.95).

FriendsWithYou Demi Mug Set 3 oz pair — Set of two coordinating blue and green ceramic espresso mugs featuring Little Cloud Boy and Fluffy ($29.95).

FriendsWithYou Stainless Steel Tumbler 13 oz — Insulated stainless steel tumbler crowned with a bright yellow star lid ($32.95).

FriendsWithYou Stainless Steel Bottle 14 oz — Rainbow-motif insulated stainless steel bottle with a rainbow character topper and blue carrying strap ($32.95).

The limited-edition Starbucks x FriendsWithYou collection arrives exclusively in participating U.S. and Canadian coffeehouses starting Nov. 24, while supplies last. Because Starbucks does not sell seasonal artist collaborations online or via mobile order-ahead in the app, your only move is to visit a standalone or licensed store in person.

Just keep in mind that the 14-ounce rainbow stainless steel bottle is a U.S. exclusive, meaning Canadian shoppers will only find five of the six pieces on shelves. And if your local store sells out by the afternoon of launch day, skip the inevitable secondary-market markups on eBay and check out the live Black Friday deals on Owala and Yeti Rambler tumblers instead.

Joseph Green is the Global Shopping Editor for Mashable. He covers VPNs, headphones, fitness gear, dating sites, streaming, and shopping events like Black Friday and Prime Day.

Joseph is also Executive Editor of Mashable's sister site, AskMen.

#500. Inside Nvidia, Not Everyone Is Celebrating Jensen Huang’s Return

Jensen Huang received a “hero’s welcome” from employees on Monday after Nvidia’s board of directors reinstated him as CEO, according to people who were present. An outspoken faction of Nvidia’s workforce had demanded his return and greeted him with chants, raucous applause, and hugs at the company’s headquarters.

But other employees were quietly stewing. Several current and former Nvidia staffers had viewed Huang’s abrupt exit earlier this month as a rare opportunity to change the “one team” corporate culture of unfettered unity and minimal bureaucracy that he had cultivated over the past three decades, according to interviews with the workers, as well as internal correspondence and social media posts reviewed by WIRED. Most spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared backlash from colleagues.

Some employees were alarmed by Huang’s alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a subordinate and another with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. But their frustrations extended beyond the CEO’s personal conduct. Current and former workers describe a culture at Nvidia in which allegedly abusive behavior was tolerated and challenging leadership was perceived as discouraged.

“Everyone agrees that mistakes were made, the question is what we are ready to forgive,” one employee wrote on an internal platform before Huang’s return. “I don’t know how comfortable I’ll be working at a place where such affairs are not taken extremely seriously.”

Another added, “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again.”

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

When Huang returned to Nvidia’s offices in California on Monday, he told employees who greeted him that he would do a better job with his second chance at CEO. (As of Monday afternoon, he had not yet sent a companywide note about his return, as he was still getting his laptop set back up.)

US president Donald Trump said he played a crucial role in convincing Nvidia's board to bring back Huang. A person close to Trump calls him an irreplaceable CEO and says they expect him to exercise better judgment going forward.

Nvidia’s board announced it will continue an independent investigation into whether Huang had been a target of foreign intelligence services and that it will double down on plans to step up corporate governance.

It’s difficult to gauge how widespread dissatisfaction with Huang’s leadership may be at Nvidia. The company’s emphasis on unity has historically made it difficult for people to openly question his leadership or choices, workers say. “There's only one team at Nvidia,” the chipmaker’s official website declares.

A public petition campaign known as Stand With Jensen garnered signatures from more than 10,000 Nvidia purported employees, according to its website. Nvidia has roughly 49,000 employees and 18,000 contractors overall, according to a person familiar with its workforce.

But inside Nvidia, one employee told colleagues that “some portion” of the signatures appeared to be “illegitimate,” noting that the names included “Satan” and media personality Mia Khalifa, who does not work at the chipmaker. The employee wrote that they found 75 suspicious names in an hour of checking. WIRED was unable to independently verify the findings. The petition’s organizers did not respond to requests for comment.

Huang’s supporters have praised how he made the company feel like a “big super family.” They credited him for minimizing bureaucracy, making himself available to staff, and supporting employees during difficult periods, including the Covid pandemic. A former employee who attended numerous meetings with Huang and other senior executives says the CEO was particularly adept at preventing bureaucratic infighting. He could detect corporate “politics and nonsense before it was even born,” says the worker.

There are also powerful financial reasons for Nvidia employees to feel loyal to Huang. His bets on chips and software for artificial intelligence have transformed Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable companies and made many longtime employees wealthy in the process.

But for some employees, the revelations about Huang’s behavior have forced them to question that loyalty. Jason Sequeira, a longtime engineering leader at Nvidia, wrote on LinkedIn last week that he ultimately couldn’t decide whether he wanted Huang back as he weighed arguments from both sides. “Some believe his contributions to Nvidia and the industry are so extraordinary that he deserves another chance,” Sequeira wrote. “Others argue that making exceptions for powerful leaders sets a dangerous precedent. … I don’t have a clear answer.”

Several current and former workers say that Huang’s management style could come off as overly harsh at times, including, for example, toward longtime colleagues he viewed as having grown complacent as Nvidia’s market value surged. Two former employees say that he regularly raised his voice at workers, sometimes in ways they found belittling.

Other employees were more concerned about whether Nvidia’s board would hold Huang accountable for allegedly misleading the directors about his affairs. “That’s something we can’t have,” one employee says.

Another source of frustration for Nvidia workers has been the growing influence of Huang’s two children and son-in-law, who all hold senior titles at the chipmaker. In March, his daughter, Madison Huang, scolded a colleague on a call with about 100 other employees, according to a participant who didn’t believe the anger was warranted. “I’m disappointed you asked that. Are you fucking stupid?” the employee recalls Madison saying in response to a question about workshops on OpenClaw technology scheduled for an upcoming Nvidia conference. “Your mom can build a claw.”

Madison and her brother, Spencer Huang, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Praveen Mhapsekar, a senior system software engineer who separated with Nvidia last week after disputes with his managers and HR, says he and colleagues stopped feeling comfortable complaining about practices that concerned them because of the trouble they believe it brought on themselves.

“This organization requires greater discipline and structured processes,” he says. One of the world’s most valuable companies “cannot be managed like a private startup operating out of a garage, where personal influence takes precedence over established procedures.”

Huang’s return doesn’t eliminate the prospect of Nvidia evolving to quell frustrations. But with internal issues more public than ever before, maybe the days of one big family all cheering along together are mostly gone.

Additional reporting by Lauren Goode and Hugo Lowell.
